Students will be introduced to the workshop method of critiquing student writing, which means you'll have the chance to have your work discussed by your peers, and vice-versa. Meets creative writing English major requirement.

title: Engaging Texts Intro
description: What are some of the ways that works of literature engage us, and in turn how can we learn to engage in various ways with literary texts: their words on the page, their imagined communities, their invented characters? How can learning about and practicing different interpretive approaches incite our readerly pleasures as well as our understanding and excitement about a work of literature’s complexity of language and form, its aesthetics, and its power both to represent and transform lives and times and places?

title: Epic and Romance
description: This course focuses on epic and romance: two genres of ancient literature which mutually inform and influence each other, and both of which formulate the foundations and inspirations of popular 21st-century genres of fiction (fantasy, science fiction, romance, among others). Readings will be selected from texts including Homer’s Iliad and Odyssey, the Irish Táin Bó Cúailnge (The Cattle Raid of Cooley), Beowulf, the Arthurian romances of Chrétien de Troyes, Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, and Geoffrey Chaucer’s Troilus and Criseyde. Our discussions will focus on the formation of the notion of heroism, and examine various stages in the development of concepts of heroism in western culture, and the cultural fantasies that accompany it. Above all, epic and romance concern themselves with the process and problematics of selfdefinition, that of the individual and of the community as a whole. The course addresses the following questions: How was reading used as a method of unifying culture in secular communities? In what ways did these narratives affirm and/or challenge societal rules? How does this literature treat figures of the nation and the king? The conventions of gender? Same as LIT 253.

title: African-American Literature II
description: Debates about the purpose, scope, and subject of black literature and culture have spanned the New Negro Renaissance, the Black Freedom Movement, the Black Arts Movement, and #BlackLivesMatter. Should black literary works establish distinctive forms or should they adhere to established Anglo-European forms? Is African American literature written for white readers or for readers of color? How can black literature be read through critical lenses largely shaped by predominantly white institutions? In what ways are black literature and the idea of black culture sutured to or separated from the material realities of anti-black racism? In this course, which considers literature written by black writers in the United States from Reconstruction to the present, we will probe important developments in the history of the United States and ask how black literary works have been received. Major figures include Ida B. Wells, W.E.B. Du Bois, Langston Hughes, Zora Neale Hurston, Richard Wright, James Baldwin, Lorraine Hansberry, Toni Morrison, and Octavia Butler. Meets post-1800 requirement for the English major. Same as AFS257.

title: Contemporary Graphic Novel
description: In this course, we will develop an historical, aesthetic, and formal understanding of contemporary graphic fiction. We'll study the genre's antecedents in early comics, the interplay of the comics and their historical and cultural contexts, graphic fiction's engagement with high art, and the formal elements of graphic texts. Readings will include comics and graphic literature from 1986 to the present, including Maus I and II, Watchmen, Fun Home, Jimmy Corrigan, Embroideries, Killing and Dying, and other graphic texts. Same as ART265. Meets contemporary requirement for the English major.

title: Law, Literature & the Person
description: This course engages with literary, philosophical, and legal notions of the person and the surprising texts that present them, from Hobbes's Leviathan to Robert Montgomery Bird's supernatural novel Sheppard Lee to Adam Winkler's We the Corporations. We will investigate central issues--personal identity, corporate personhood, and slavery--via literary texts, Supreme Court decisions, and contemporary culture including the TV series Severance. More broadly, we will attend to the intersection of law and literature and the ways the two fields can inform each other in unexpected ways.

title: What is Queer Literature?
description: What does it mean to read queerly? What distinguishes a queer novel from a novel with queer characters? What constitutes the queer literary canon? This course invites students to grapple with these questions while exploring a wide range of literature similarly invested in queer experiences. Drawing on queer/feminist theory & criticism, we will consider the queerness of literature and the literature of queerness. You can expect to encounter a variety of classic and contemporary voices in this class, including but not limited to: Audre Lorde, Ocean Vuong, James Baldwin, Brandon Taylor, Carmen Maria Machado, Leslie Feinberg, Torrey Peters, and Sarah Waters.

title: Harlem Renaissance
description: The Harlem Renaissance represented an explosion of Black cultural, economic and political activity in the first and second decades of the twentieth century. Fifty years after emancipation, African Americans were still struggling for equality and acceptance from White America. The cultural products of the period -- events, writings, music, theater, and literature, for example -- represented a desire by African Americans to forge a new identity and find a place in American democracy. We will explore how African Americans used these cultural products to express their history, experiences, predicaments, hopes and racial consciousness and pride. In this course, we will examine some of the writers and the texts of the period. Same as AFS/AMS 316.

title: Indig/Colonial Entanglements
description: Whereas Indigenous peoples are marginalized in traditional accounts of US literature and history, this course foregrounds the textual legacy of the early, often violent entanglement of Native and colonial people. How did Indigenous writers represent themselves and their nations, and how did they recount and resist colonialism and genocide? How did encounters with Native people lead colonial, European, and US writers to see the world differently? We will read a wide variety of genres, some traditionally “literary” (memoirs, plays, fiction), some less so (colonial sales pitches, treaties, transcribed oratory). We’ll read texts with close attention to how they use language and how they frame Indigeneity, colonialism, cultural difference, and more. Fulfills the pre-1800 requirement for the English major. Same as LIT 371.

title: Playwriting II
description: An upper level writing workshop, exploring advanced concepts and theories of writing for the stage. Students will complete the first draft of a full-length play. Prerequisite: TND 283 or instructor permission. Same as TND 383.

title: Writing Creative Nonfiction
description: A workshop for students ready to find their voices in a genre that claims to tell the truth without making it up. As a term, “nonfiction” says what it is by saying what it isn’t, but if nonfiction is anything that is not fiction, where are its boundaries? Where does its creative dimension take shape? We will read works of contemporary memoir, essay, and experimental nonfiction, and students will write and significantly revise two or more nonfiction texts that report, interrogate, and play with the truth. Permission of instructor required. Meets creative writing English major requirement.

title: Advanced Poetry Workshop
description: Writing and sequencing a large group of poems is exciting. It gives you the opportunity to envision a small project and consider the ways to sustain both your own and the reader’s attention, line after line, poem after poem. It can also be a process of surprise as your vision at the start might change as the work itself demands something new over the course of time. This course is an advanced workshop for writers interested in completing an extended poetry manuscript. You will draft, revise, and polish a creative thesis of 15 pages which will represent the culmination of your study of the genre. At the beginning of the semester, we will read and discuss essays on poetics, as well as poetry collections that vary thematically, formally, and in their approach to language. We will take that vocabulary of praise and critique and apply it to peer work twice in the semester. Early on and mid-semester, we will meet individually to discuss questions, concerns, or new inspirations. You will leave the course with enough poems for a chapbook and—for those thinking seriously about poetry after F&M—the groundwork for further poetic exploration. Permission of the instructor required.

title: Contemporary Indian Literature
description: Although fiction by Indians writing in English since the 1980s is probably best known on the world stage, Indians have been prolific producers of literature in English in a variety of genres for the last two centuries. Through exposure to fiction, poetry, and non-fiction, this course will offer a taste of the tremendous energy and vitality which characterizes literary production in India today. Students will also develop a picture of the fraught place English has occupied in India from the pre-Independence period to the first decade of this century. Meets 400-level seminar requirement for the English major or the contemporary literature requirement for majors in the creative writing track, or fulfills the NW or WP requirement. The course cannot count for more than one of the English major requirements. Permission of the instructor is required. Same as LIT494

title: Intro to Film & Media Studies
description: This course introduces students to the critical analysis of cinema and its formal elements. It provides the analytical tools and vocabulary to talk about the aesthetics of cinema and the ways in which film form has cultural, social, and political dimensions. It will serve not only to highlight and to expose students to a variety of modes and styles of filmmaking, but also to help students develop a more engaged, critical eye for viewing media. Additional required screening time one evening per week.

title: Film History
description: An introduction to the history of motion pictures from the 1890s through the present day. Surveys both the evolution of popular movies and influential artistic and rhetorical counter-currents, including "national" film movements, experimental cinema, and documentary. Formerly FLM 215.

title: Introduction to Filmmaking
description: This course teaches filmmaking fundamentals through a series of projects that focus on motivated camera work, lighting for moving image, video editing, and the creative use of sound with video. Students will also explore a range of conceptual and methodological approaches in creative film practice. Prerequisite for subsequent filmmaking courses. Formerly FLM 226.

title: Introduction to Filmmaking
description: This course teaches filmmaking fundamentals through a series of projects that focus on motivated camera work, lighting for moving image, video editing, and the creative use of sound with video. Students will also explore a range of conceptual and methodological approaches in creative film practice. Prerequisite for subsequent filmmaking courses. Formerly FLM 226.

title: Narrative Filmmaking
description: An intermediate filmmaking course dedicated to the art and craft of narrative production. This course focuses on creative process, collaborative filmmaking, and cinematic storytelling. Coursework consists of readings, film responses, creative exercises, and a final film project. Students in this class will learn a range of aesthetic, technical, and logistical skills in order to complete an original short fiction film by the end of the semester. Prerequisite: FLM 126/226. Repeatable by permission of the instructor.

title: Religion and Film
description: How does religion look, feel, and sound on film? How do movies mediate and produce religious subjects? And what might we learn about religion and religion-making through attention to the particularities of cinema? This course looks at religion in film. More specifically, we examine religion and film with three different foci: (1) the representation of religion in cinema; (2) the formation of religious subjects through movies; (3) religion-making in the techniques, production, and distribution of film. We will approach film not only as a potent medium for the global circulation of religious traditions but also as a generative site for analyzing the sensorial and affective power of religion more broadly. Same as RST 279.

title: 16mm Filmmaking
description: This course introduces students to analog photochemical filmmaking practices and processes. Working with 16mm film, students in the course will explore the potential of non-digital moving images by filming, hand-processing, hand-painting/scratching/manipulating, and editing celluloid film. Coursework primarily consists of a series of creative projects. Prerequisite: FLM 126 or permission of the instructor. A materials fee of $75 is required.

title: Ecological Cinema
description: This course explores how narrative, documentary and experimental filmmakers approach making films about (and with) the environment. Students will engage with ecological film through discussions, readings, writing and creative practice. Students will encounter works by Daïchi Saïto, Michael Snow, James Benning and more, while considering how film can respond to the climate crisis and the aesthetics of ecology.

title: Writing for Television
description: Combining workshop, lecture, class discussion, and in-class writing exercises, this course explores the fundamentals of the art and craft of writing for television. Over the length of the semester we will investigate the nature and meaning of "drama" and "visual narrative" as functioning on the small screen. We will do this in part through the examination of format, style, structure, and needs of the network/streaming sites for both a comedy (30 minute) and a drama (60 minute) series. We will also study the basics of scene building, conflict, character, and dialogue by writing a draft of both a “spec” script and an original pilot. Students will develop and complete an outline and first draft of a television pilot on their own and in collaborative groups. Same as TND/ENG 387.

title: Elementary French II
description: Continuation of FRN101. Prerequisite: FRN 101 or placement.

title: Elementary French II
description: Continuation of FRN101. Prerequisite: FRN 101 or placement.

title: Elementary French II
description: Continuation of FRN101. Prerequisite: FRN 101 or placement.

title: Intermediate French II
description: Continuation of FRN 201. Perfection of oral, aural and written language skills. Coursework may include discussion of current events in the Francophone world, based on a variety of texts from both literary and contemporary digital and print sources. Emphasis is on developing linguistic and cultural competence. Prerequisite: FRN 201 or placement. This course requires no textbook but does have a $45 materials fee.

title: The Age of Enlightenment
description: "What is Enlightenment?" This question was posed by Immanuel Kant in 1784 and has intrigued historians since. Was the Enlightenment a unified body of thought? What was the goal of the "Enlightenment project"? How did it impact more than the history of ideas, to influence cultural practices and the daily lives? What was its relationship to contemporary political systems? This course will explore Enlightenment debates and developments. Topics for discussion will include the birth of the intellectual; the idea of the public sphere; religious enlightenment and secularism; race, slavery, and colonialism; the gender politics of the Enlightenment; Enlightenment and revolution; and the modern legacy of the Enlightenment. Same as HIS/STS/WGS 224.

title: Engaging w/Francophone Wrld II
description: This course introduces students to different types of French and Francophone texts. We begin by learning reading strategies and the techniques used in literary and textual analysis, then we learn to produce written and oral analyses of these texts using the forms common to French literary analysis. By the end of the course, students will be able to identify principal characteristics of major genres, write analytical commentaries on prose and poetry, and will be prepared to read unfamiliar French texts critically. Prerequisite: FRN 301, placement or permission of the instructor.

title: Medicine in Literature
description: This course explores the representations of illness and care in French and francophone literatures, from the seventeenth to the twenty- first century. Each century will be represented by a celebrated classic text, allowing us to see how writers have depicted illness, medical practices, and the relationships between patients and caregivers. We will consider how literature reflects and shapes ideas about health, suffering, and healing, and how these perceptions have changed over time in French and francophone cultures. This course invites students to see literature as a lens on medical knowledge, social attitudes, and the human experience of illness. Prerequisite: FRN 302 or permission of instructor. Same as AFS 378

title: Elementary German II
description: Students expand their understanding of the question “What is German?” through topics such as daily routines, food and restaurants, fairy tales, and immigration. By reading and discussing films, short texts, and a full-length youth novel, students gain knowledge of German culture and society, improve their communicative competence, and develop skills needed to negotiate a variety of cultural settings. Prerequisite: GER 101 or placement. Offered every Spring.

title: Intermediate German II
description: In this course, students will build on the solid foundation of German they have previously acquired, sharpening their skills in the four critical areas of speaking, listening, reading, and writing. The thematic focus of the course will be the history of twentieth-century Germany with a special focus on the experiences of people of African descent in German society, including the following topics: the history of Germany in the 1920s, 1950s and today, with an emphasis on the experiences of people of African descent; children and children’s literature in 20th-century Germany; famous Germans and their contributions to the realms of sport, music, art, literature in the 20th century, including prominent people of African descent; and the history of interactions between Germans and people of African descent during the age of imperialism, the Third Reich, and the years following the Second World War. Prerequisite: GER 201 or placement. Offered every Spring.

title: Reading Berlin, 1920/2020
prereq: GER 301 OR GER 302 OR GER 325 OR GER 327 OR GER 340 OR GER 341 OR GER 342 OR GER 343 OR GER 370 OR GER 371 OR GER 372 OR GER 373 OR GER 374 OR GER 375 OR GER 376 OR GER 377 OR GER 378 OR GER 379 OR GER 390 OR GER 391
description: What does it mean to read a city? If we read Berlin, what can we learn about German history, culture, and identity, past and present? These are the questions we will seek to answer as we explore the city of Berlin and its turbulent past century. We will immerse ourselves in Berlin across two centuries: turbulent, exciting Berlin of the 1920s and vibrant, multicultural Berlin of the 2020s. Students will develop their intermediate-to-advanced proficiency in German while engaging with texts in a variety of genres (literature, history, journalism), as well as maps, films, architecture and a streaming series that will bring the city of Berlin to life. Prerequisite: one 300-level German course or permission.

title: Power and Politics
description: This course provides an introduction to the field of Political Science, including the main concepts and themes related to power and politics at the individual, community, state, and international levels. Questions include: Why do we need states and governments? Whose interests are represented in political systems? When do different groups gain representation and power? Does democracy really help people, or are there other forms of government that work better? To what extent does the form of government affect the behavior of politicians? At the end of the course, students will have an introduction to the systems, institutions, and behaviors that inform politics around the world. Not open to students who have taken GOV 100 or GOV 120.

title: Understanding Public Policy
prereq: GOV 100 OR GOV 120 OR PBH 251 OR GOV 171 OR GOV 101
description: Focus on government activity in a variety of public policy areas, the structural and political contexts of debates over alternative policy strategies, and approaches to understanding public policy. Policy areas examined include the national budget and entitlements, science and technology, and education. Prerequisite: GOV100 or GOV120 or GOV 101/171 or PBH251.

title: Understanding Public Policy
prereq: GOV 100 OR GOV 120 OR PBH 251 OR GOV 171 OR GOV 101
description: Focus on government activity in a variety of public policy areas, the structural and political contexts of debates over alternative policy strategies, and approaches to understanding public policy. Policy areas examined include the national budget and entitlements, science and technology, and education. Prerequisite: GOV100 or GOV120 or GOV 101/171 or PBH251.

title: International Security
description: The overarching goal of this class is to introduce you to the major topics and debates within the field and to give you the skills and knowledge to identify and critique the assumptions that are often embedded in discussions about international security. The course begins with the traditional question of why nations fight and whether the nature of war is changing, and then moves through a range of contemporary challenges to security, including nuclear weapons, terrorism, migration, and climate change.

title: Political Research
prereq: GOV 100 OR GOV 101 OR GOV 171 OR GOV 120 OR GOV 130
description: Empirical investigation in political science; scientific inquiry in political science; problems of logical induction; selecting and formulating a research problem; functions and types of research design; analysis of data, both qualitative and quantitative. Primarily for government majors; should be completed no later than first semester of junior year. Prerequisite: GOV 101 or GOV 171 or GOV 100 or GOV 120 or GOV 130.

title: Political Research
prereq: GOV 100 OR GOV 101 OR GOV 171 OR GOV 120 OR GOV 130
description: Empirical investigation in political science; scientific inquiry in political science; problems of logical induction; selecting and formulating a research problem; functions and types of research design; analysis of data, both qualitative and quantitative. Primarily for government majors; should be completed no later than first semester of junior year. Prerequisite: GOV 101 or GOV 171 or GOV 100 or GOV 120 or GOV 130.

title: Politics of Terrorism
description: One objective of this course is to help you develop a more nuanced and multi-faceted understanding of terrorism: its history (including the very fact that it has a history--contrary to the predominant impression in the U.S., terrorism did not begin on 9/11); why and how the tactic has been used by a variety of groups pursuing very different goals; and why even its definition is a matter of intense political dispute. We will explore different explanations of the causes of terrorism and examine many of the ongoing debates in the field. We will then seek to apply those insights to a range of terrorist group case studies.

title: Global Democracy Lab
description: This lab gives students a space to learn about—and practice—democracy in its many forms. The course is organized around three ways of "doing" democracy: representative, deliberative, and participatory. Students read about each then put them into practice through activities like climate assemblies and participatory budgeting. Along the way, we engage local and global experts to learn what's being done to deepen democracy on campus, in Lancaster, and around the world.

title: Public Policy Implementation
description: This upper-level course in public policy focuses on three core goals: understanding how policy is implemented after it becomes law, learning how to assess and analyze the state of a given set of public policies, and understanding the institutional landscape of the policy making and implementation process. Students will gain hands-on experience analyzing contemporary policy dilemmas and learning the skills required to be a working policy professional. Prerequisite: GOV200.

title: F&M in Harrisburg Practicum
description: This practicum is designed to give students hands-on experience working in state government or state-related public affairs. Students will spend a minimum of 96 hours during the semester at an internship in Harrisburg. They will also meet once a week on campus to consider various aspects of Pennsylvania government and reflect on the work they are doing in their internships. The practicum is offered every spring.

title: F&M in Harrisburg Practicum
description: This practicum is designed to give students hands-on experience working in state government or state-related public affairs. Students will spend a minimum of 96 hours during the semester at an internship in Harrisburg. They will also meet once a week on campus to consider various aspects of Pennsylvania government and reflect on the work they are doing in their internships. The practicum is offered every spring.

title: Civil Rights & Civil Liberties
description: Explores civil rights and liberties in the American system, with emphasis on current problems and recent Court decisions. Prerequisite: GOV101 or GOV171 or GOV100. Same as WGS 315.

title: Civil Rights & Civil Liberties
description: Explores civil rights and liberties in the American system, with emphasis on current problems and recent Court decisions. Prerequisite: GOV101 or GOV171 or GOV100. Same as WGS 315.

title: Making Sense of Putin's Russia
description: This course examines the structural factors that led to the weakening of the Soviet Union in the 1970s and 1980s; its last leader, Mikhail Gorbachev's attempts to reinvigorate his country and its communist system through his policies of perestroika and glasnost'; how these reforms engendered the collapse of the Berlin Wall and the USSR; the creation of the modern Russian regime under Boris Yeltsin, whose presidency witnessed unprecedented corruption, kleptocracy, staggering inflation, and the emergence of the Russian mafiya; and the transition of power to Vladimir Putin. We conduct a deep dive into Putin's attempts to “make Russia great again” by embracing the tactics of his security state (KGB) roots and reasserting control over territories that had formerly belonged to the Russian Empire and the Soviet Union. We examine Putin's crackdown on the free press; civil rights; civil society/NGOs, and the wars he unleashed on Chechnya, Georgia, and Ukraine. We examine the evolution of youth culture; the position of women, members of the LGBT community, and non- Russian ethnic groups; the rise of the right-wing; climate change, and environmental problems related to Russia's fossil-fuel-based mono- economy; and topics of geopolitical and economic significance to the US government and its allies.Same as HIS/IST/RUS319.

title: Internationl Environmental Law
prereq: ENE 216 OR STS 216 OR GOV 200 OR PUB 200
description: This course examines principles and instruments of International Environmental Law (IEL), beginning with the nature and sources of IEL and an introduction to the key actors and agencies involved in global environmental governance. Focusing on the development of regimes addressing a range of environmental issues, the course also addresses implementation and state responsibility for environmental harm and dispute resolution. Topics explored include climate change and atmospheric pollution; the law of the sea and protection of the marine environment; international regulation of toxic substances; conservation of nature, ecosystems and biodiversity; and the intersection of international trade and environmental protection. Students will examine treaties and case law first-hand, and represent vested interests in a simulated negotiation of a multilateral environmental agreement. Prerequisite: ENE/STS 216 or GOV/PUB 200. Same as ENE 320.

title: Rights and Representations
description: This course explores controversies about the First Amendment (or freedom of expression), particularly in relation to race and gender, in the past and in the contemporary US. This class examines the categorical exceptions to the First Amendment and then focuses on the following case studies: hate speech in higher education, racial and sexual harassment in employment, and harassment in cyberspace. Same as AMS/WGS 358.

title: LGBT+ Human Rights in Chg Wrld
description: Are LGBT+ rights human Rights? Special rights? What protections do members of the LGBT+ community have? What protections should they have? How do countries vary in the protection or persecution of LGBT+ individuals? Utilizing data from the F&M Global Barometers (in addition to other sources), students will apply this knowledge to creating LGBT+ asylum profiles for various countries. Same as WGS370.

title: Theories of Law and Punishment
description: Why do we punish? How has punishment changed over time in the United States? Who can punish? How does punishment interact with violence? How does punishment intersect with constructions and experiences of race and class? And what continuities and changes can we see across penal theory from the 18th century to today? This course moves chronologically through penal theory and practice in the United States, beginning with the roots of the penitentiary, convict labor, police, and the prison. Throughout we will probe the relationship between law and violence--including violence differentially distributed by race and class. This course merges historical, theoretical, and legal readings to understand law and punishment across time. Satisfies the Political Theory Course for GOV majors.

title: Law of Sports
description: This course will examine the relationship between the business of sports and the legal framework in which leagues, teams, and players operate. Included in the course will be an examination of the legal and business issues arising from antitrust regulation of sports, the impact of gambling platforms and sports books, labor-management relations, regulation of sports agents and government support and regulation of stadium financing. The course will also utilize a “case studies” format to probe legal and business disputes in the industry including the PGA Tour-LIV Golf competition, the MLB collective bargaining re-negotiation and the lockout-strike strategies, the business threat posed by criminal prosecution of professional athletes for violation of league gambling rules, and the impact of new name, image and likeness rules on college and pro sports.

title: East/West & Decolonial Theory
description: This is a course in decolonial and political theory that will explore the historical legacy of colonialism and the ongoing conflict between the so-called east/west. Through a range of texts, we will analyze and critique the major theoretical and cultural origins of various contemporary social-political phenomena that are connected to the east/west conflict, including war on terror, the rise of ISIS, and the militarization of everyday life throughout the world. Through these texts, students will be prepared to discuss a wide range of foundational issues in decolonial and political theory: Colonialism/coloniality, orientalism, discourse theory, liberation philosophy, the subbaltern, hybridity, difference, ambiguity, interstitiallity, race and racialization, and many more. Satisfies the Political Theory Course for GOV majors.

title: Health Policy
description: This course investigates domestic and global health policy issues. We will survey health care and health systems, focusing on health care spending, insurance, and health outcomes. Students will also examine ethical dilemmas and debates within health policy. We will ask what role health policy can play in addressing health disparities. Two questions infuse our deliberations: what can the government do to shape the health of individuals and what should it do? Formerly GOV 410. Same as PBH 380.

title: Health Policy
description: This course investigates domestic and global health policy issues. We will survey health care and health systems, focusing on health care spending, insurance, and health outcomes. Students will also examine ethical dilemmas and debates within health policy. We will ask what role health policy can play in addressing health disparities. Two questions infuse our deliberations: what can the government do to shape the health of individuals and what should it do? Formerly GOV 410. Same as PBH 380.

title: Presidential Character
description: This course examines the role that individual politicians, particularly American presidents, play in American politics. We examine concepts such as presidential leadership and presidential character. A primary goal of the course is to understand what types of individuals are likely to become president and which individual traits successful presidents likely to possess. Prerequisite: GOV100.

title: Human Rights/Human Wrongs
description: This course is structured as a senior seminar. It focuses on human rights and human wrongs in general, emphasizing political asylum in the United States. The major component of the course, aside from the weekly seminar readings and discussions, centers on the political asylum project. Students work on a political asylum case in the context of a community partnership. Students work in groups and compile evidence, testimony, and detainee affidavits that are used in an immigration court of law for the political asylum detainee's case. Students have direct hands-on experience working with asylum seekers currently incarcerated in an INS detention facility. Students present and evaluate individual cases in a mock trial.

title: Elem Ancient Greek II
description: GRK102 continues the study of the basic grammar and syntax of classical Greek. Prerequisite: GRK101 or placement.

title: Nazi Germany
description: Even eight decades after its collapse, the Third Reich continues to pose compelling questions about democracies' vulnerability to dictatorship and the ideologies and practice of genocide. This course will explore the culture, economics, and politics of Germany before, during, and after the Nazi dictatorship with special attention to class, gender, propaganda, race, religion, sexuality, and state violence. How and why did the Weimar experiment fail? What were the consequences for Europeans, Jews, the Roma and Sinti, colonized populations, and the global world order? How has the Third Reich, including its collaborators, opponents, and victims, been remembered? Same as HIS 275

title: Introduction to Art History
description: An introduction to Western art and architecture, including Europe from antiquity to the present and North America from the colonial period to the present. Students learn skills of visual analysis, writing, and reasoning, and gain an understanding of the social, political, cultural, and spiritual contexts for art making across time and space. Formerly ART 103.

title: Introduction to Asian Art
description: An introduction to the visual culture of East Asia (China and Japan), including a unit in Indian Buddhist art. The course examines a small number of topics with an aim to introduce basic art historical method through the close study of key monuments. Formerly ART 105.

title: Intro to Architecture II
description: A survey of architecture from the fifteenth century to the present. The course aims to give a thorough understanding of architectural discourse from the Renaissance to current movements. Special focus will be given to the effects of industrialization, urbanization, globalization and the dialectics of modernity. In addition to learning the parade of styles and architectural innovations, we will consider the art of building as the highest form of human inquiry within the public realm. Moreover, we will learn how to read the language of architecture, its parts, inherent qualities, contradictions and formal principles. Formerly ART 123.

title: Antisemitism & Visual Culture
description: Many of the most enduring anti-Jewish images were carved into the stone of medieval churches, and they remain there today. This course follows those images and their descendants from medieval sculpture and manuscripts through Nazi propaganda, political cartoons, and social media, paying close attention to how buildings and cities have marked Jews as outsiders. Students will learn to trace a motif across centuries, separating real lines of descent from coincidental resemblance, and will apply these tools to contested contemporary cases, including images connected to Israel, where scholars disagree about where criticism and satire end and antisemitism begins. Same as JST174.

title: 18th- and 19th-Century Art
description: A survey of European art from 1750 to 1900, including such movements as Neoclassicism, Romanticism, and Impressionism and such artists as Constable, Delacriox, and Van Gogh. We will consider art, architecture, and decorative arts in their historical and cultural contexts, examining such themes as the significance of landscape in an industrializing world, the cultural competition of World's Fairs, and the fashion for Orientalism. Prerequisite: No prerequisite, but HAA 103 is strongly recommended. Formerly ART 241.

title: Classical Chinese Painting
description: This course introduces the most important genres and themes in Chinese painting from roughly the mid-fourth to the end of the fourteenth century. Topics given special attention include the illustration of narrative and lyric poetry, the rise of monumental landscape painting and the ideal of reclusion, the painting theory of scholars, imperial patronage, Ch'an (Zen) Buddhist painting, and the dynamic interaction between painting and calligraphy. Formerly ART 281.

title: American Photography
description: Soon after the invention of photography, photographic images quickly constituted much of visual culture—either national or global. Sometimes photographs were made with high artistic intention, but, far more often, not. This seminar will examine diverse topics in 19th and 20th-century American photographic history, from vernacular images produced for the masses (daguerreotypes, tintypes, snapshots) to what have now become nearly iconic photographs produced either for documentary purposes or to make artistic, self-expressive statements. We will consider the work of unknown makers as well as that produced by celebrated photographers such as Alfred Stieglitz, Edward Weston, Walker Evans, Ansel Adams, Dorothea Lange, Robert Frank, and Robert Adams. Same as AMS 353. Formerly ART 353.

title: Ancient Greek Sculpture
prereq: CLS 115 OR HAA 115 OR CLS 117 OR HAA 117 OR HAA 103
description: Greek sculptors created models of the human figure that still shape how we envision ideal beauty today. But whose bodies did they choose to immortalize and why? We will examine marble and bronze sculptures within the original cultural context and consider shifting norms of physical perfection in antiquity. Throughout the course, we will ask how Greek sculpture continues to inform modern ideas of beauty, the body, and the look of public sculpture. Prerequisite: CLS 115, CLS 117, HAA 103 or permission of instructor. Same as CLS 371.

title: Urban Life in the Middle East
description: This course follows the history of urban life in the Middle East from the rise of Islam to the modern day. We follow the emergence of a unique Islamic urban model, reflected in examples like the Round City of Baghdad and medieval Cairo, and trace its evolution through encounters with globalization, European modernity and colonialism, and the fossil fuel economy. Through the investigation of textual material, city plans, architectural drawings, and GIS mapping, the students will acquire deep insight into the history of the region and the methodology of urban history. Same as ENE/HIS374.

title: Europe in 20th Century World
description: Frames the First World War, Russian Revolution, National Socialism, Second World War, Holocaust, Cold War, decolonization, immigration, European unity, 1968 movements, 1989 revolutions, and Yugoslav wars within a global context with emphasis on themes of democracy, socialism/communism, fascism, nationalism, racism, gender and sexual identity, and postwar reconciliation.

title: Modern Middle East
description: Introduction to the history of the Middle East (including Iran and Turkey) from the late 18th century to the present. We will focus on colonialism, the rise of nationalism, and the major ideologies that have mobilized communities across the region.

title: History of Colonial Latin Amer
description: Survey of Latin America from pre-Conquest times to the present. Begins with historical backgrounds of indigenous societies as well as Spain, Portugal, and Africa before 1492, followed by an examination of the conquest and colonial period through independence. The course focuses on the contributions of these major cultural groups in the formation of colonial Latin American society and culture. Same as AFS 131.

title: American History, 1491-1865
description: This course traces the history of North America from European contact and conquest to the end of the American Civil War by analyzing ten significant moments. Among other events, we shall look in depth at the rebellion by enslaved laborers in colonial South Carolina, the publication of Common Sense in 1775, the Ratification of the Federal Constitution, the first women’s rights convention at Seneca Falls, the “Trail of Tears,” and John Brown’s raid on Harpers Ferry. Along with some scholarly articles, students will read an extensive collection of primary sources to unpack these events.

title: U.S. and the Modern World
description: This course traces the rise of the United States since the Civil War, as an urban, industrial society marked by deep racial and ethnic cleavages. Besides studying movements and legal struggles for equality, it examines America's role as a world power, from intervention n Latin America through two world wars, the Cold War, and Vietnam. Students can expect to use primary documents and engage in debates.

title: Hist of East & Southern Africa
description: Introduction to major themes in the history of East, Central, and Southern Africa from the Bantu migration through the Rwandan genocide. Emphasizes social, political, and religious change in pre-colonial Africa, and resistance to slavery and colonialism. Students use primary sources to explore historical problems. Final unit explores the legacy of colonialism in the 1994 Rwandan genocide. Same as AFS 142.

title: Democracy and Fascism
description: Battles between fascism and democracy have cost millions of lives, but their echoes resound as fascist ideas and practices resurge in contemporary politics. How has democracy evolved over millennia across the globe? Is it in crisis today? What does examining race, nationalism, gender, sexuality, economic crisis, propaganda, and leadership cults tell us about how fascism achieves and maintains power? How have democracies withstood fascist assault in the past, and how can they defend themselves today? Same as IST 223.

title: The Age of Enlightenment
description: "What is Enlightenment?" This question was posed by Immanuel Kant in 1784 and has intrigued historians since. Was the Enlightenment a unified body of thought? What was the goal of the "Enlightenment project"? How did it impact more than the history of ideas, to influence cultural practices and the daily lives? What was its relationship to contemporary political systems? This course will explore Enlightenment debates and developments. Topics for discussion will include the birth of the intellectual; the idea of the public sphere; religious enlightenment and secularism; race, slavery, and colonialism; the gender politics of the Enlightenment; Enlightenment and revolution; and the modern legacy of the Enlightenment. Same as FRN/STS/WGS 224.

title: History Workshop
description: Trains students in the methodology and practice of history, in preparation for seminar research and reading and the scholarly practice of history. The two principal objectives of the History Workshop are “historiographical literacy” (a reasonably comprehensive grasp of historical approaches, methodologies, and schools of analysis) and learning the “mechanics of doing history” (how to research and write history, including ethical and practical issues of archival work, library and web use, the mechanics of citation, and more). Classes center on critical analysis of readings, textual interpretation of primary documents, and library activities. Open to all students, but priority is granted to majors and minors. Should be taken during the sophomore or junior year.

title: Nazi Germany
description: Even eight decades after its collapse, the Third Reich continues to pose compelling questions about democracies' vulnerability to dictatorship and the ideologies and practice of genocide. This course will explore the culture, economics, and politics of Germany before, during, and after the Nazi dictatorship with special attention to class, gender, propaganda, race, religion, sexuality, and state violence. How and why did the Weimar experiment fail? What were the consequences for Europeans, Jews, the Roma and Sinti, colonized populations, and the global world order? How has the Third Reich, including its collaborators, opponents, and victims, been remembered? Same as GST 275

title: The Urban Citizen (CBL)
description: In this community-based learning course students will have the opportunity to engage in study and experiential activities around civic engagement and social issues. They will examine the lives of documented and undocumented citizens as well as “returning citizens” (who are formerly incarcerated) and newly arrived citizens. We will consider, among other things, gender and poverty, race relations, affordable housing, urban economies, crime and policing, schools, refugees, and environmentalism in an urban setting. Students will integrate their academic studies with direct community engagement work of their choice in Lancaster. Same as AMS/AFS/WGS 279.

title: History of Medicine
description: The history of medicine with particular attention to American medicine. The relationship between medicine and society is studied in its historical context. We look in detail at some trends in modern medicine and the current debate over national health care policy in light of the history of medicine. Same as NSP/STS311.

title: N. American Environ History
description: Examination of various approaches to American environmental and ecological history. Focuses on ways in which the physical and biological world have affected human history and on ways in which American social and political organizations, economic activities, cultural values and scientific theories have shaped Americans' interactions with nature. Selected case studies from American environmental history, with emphasis on the 17th through the 20th centuries. Same as ENE/STS 312.

title: Making Sense of Putin's Russia
description: This course examines the structural factors that led to the weakening of the Soviet Union in the 1970s and 1980s; its last leader, Mikhail Gorbachev's attempts to reinvigorate his country and its communist system through his policies of perestroika and glasnost'; how these reforms engendered the collapse of the Berlin Wall and the USSR; the creation of the modern Russian regime under Boris Yeltsin, whose presidency witnessed unprecedented corruption, kleptocracy, staggering inflation, and the emergence of the Russian mafiya; and the transition of power to Vladimir Putin. We conduct a deep dive into Putin's attempts to “make Russia great again” by embracing the tactics of his security state (KGB) roots and reasserting control over territories that had formerly belonged to the Russian Empire and the Soviet Union. We examine Putin's crackdown on the free press; civil rights; civil society/NGOs, and the wars he unleashed on Chechnya, Georgia, and Ukraine. We examine the evolution of youth culture; the position of women, members of the LGBT community, and non- Russian ethnic groups; the rise of the right-wing; climate change, and environmental problems related to Russia's fossil-fuel-based mono- economy; and topics of geopolitical and economic significance to the US government and its allies. Same as GOV/IST/RUS 319

title: 20th Century US Business
description: Roughly a century ago President Calvin Coolidge once suggested that "the business of the American people is business." This course takes him at his word and teaches students about the history of the United States by focusing on the development and structure of business from 1900 to the present. Students will investigate the emergence of the United States as the world's leading economic power, the broad influence of big business on American work and institutions, the development of a mixed economy through the New Deal and World War II; the importance of consumerism in postwar America; diminished American competitiveness in the 1970s; the rise of neoliberalism and financialization; and the influence of economic theory on policy making. Same as Bos372

title: American Communities
description: This course focuses on the principal methods and paradigms used in conceptualizing, researching, and writing on “communities.” To do this we will focus on “community,” how communities vary in form and function, and what draws people into and away from various social groupings; we will study communities on their own terms, and within the wider context of American cultural and political life, with a special focus on F&M campus communities. Students will employ different methods in studying campus communities. Counts for the WGS major and minor. Not open to students who have taken AMS 350. Same as AMS/WGS 373.

title: Urban Life in the Middle East
description: This course follows the history of urban life in the Middle East from the rise of Islam to the modern day. We follow the emergence of a unique Islamic urban model, reflected in examples like the Round City of Baghdad and medieval Cairo, and trace its evolution through encounters with globalization, European modernity and colonialism, and the fossil fuel economy. Through the investigation of textual material, city plans, architectural drawings, and GIS mapping, the students will acquire deep insight into the history of the region and the methodology of urban history. Same as ENE/HAA 374.

title: Global Reproductive Politics
description: This seminar introduces students to the history of sexuality and gender in Latin America as the study of identities and relationships of power that have changed over time. In addition to providing a foundation in current historical research and theoretical debates about sexuality as a category of analysis, the course will explore research methodologies using a wide range of sources, from censuses, oral accounts, diaries, letters, ecclesiastical accounts, judicial records, health reports, advertising, comic books, and other print media. It is useful to be able to read Spanish for this course, but not necessary. The seminar will emphasize the role of sexuality in the creation of diverse historical experiences of women and men, and its importance in the construction of varied masculinities and femininities within Latin America. The course will also explore how sexuality and gender have intersected with ethnicity, race, and social class in the creation of distinct Latin American societies and cultures. Same as WGS475. Prerequisite: HIS260 (recommended but not required).

title: Mindfulness,Meaning &Wellbeing
description: This course explores the practice of mindfulness through an interdisciplinary lens. Students will develop the knowledge, skills, and competencies necessary to incorporate practices that positively impact their wellbeing into their every-day lives while exploring the ways in which people make meaning of their life experiences. This course takes a multidisciplinary and experiential approach, connecting students to resources on campus and in the broader community, designed to positively impact students’ success in and out of the classroom.

title: Leadership
description: What does effective leadership look like during intense periods of technological, political, economic, social, and environmental change and disruption? This course is part theory and part experiential. Students will indeed dive into theories of leadership, but they will also practice what it means to lead during chaotic times with diverse teams.

title: Migration in Lancaster
description: This 0.5 credit course invites students to develop or continue a research project focusing on migrants, refugees, or the question of welcome in Lancaster using a Humanities-based approach. The course will meet for one hour per week for guidance and to share feedback on projects; the remaining time will be spent in independent research in the community. Research findings will be shared during the closing Reckoning with Lancaster symposium.

title: Entrepreneurial Discovery
description: Entrepreneurs are society’s stereotypical problem solvers. Entrepreneurial Discovery is an experiential learning course in which students advance startup concepts by leveraging entrepreneurial problem-solving methodologies as well as visitors. The goal is for students to learn to navigate challenges associated with bringing innovative change to society in any sector. Learning objectives: 1. Design, test, measure, and iterate hypothesis-driven startup experiments. 2. Weigh conflicting experimental outcomes to decide next steps for advancing or pivoting. 3. Turn lessons from visitors’ real world experience into actionable insights. Same as INT 365.

title: Intro to International Studies
description: IST200 is an introduction to global issues through the multidisciplinary perspective that informs International Studies. The course provides students with key vocabulary and various frameworks of analysis as they examine globalization, migration, cross-cultural encounters, human rights, security, conflict, sustainability, and related issues. Organized around a core set of readings, the course features lectures with faculty in several departments and across the divisions of the College.

title: Democracy and Fascism
description: Battles between fascism and democracy have cost millions of lives, but their echoes resound as fascist ideas and practices resurge in contemporary politics. How has democracy evolved over millennia across the globe? Is it in crisis today? What does examining race, nationalism, gender, sexuality, economic crisis, propaganda, and leadership cults tell us about how fascism achieves and maintains power? How have democracies withstood fascist assault in the past, and how can they defend themselves today? Same as HIS 223.

title: Making Sense of Putin's Russia
description: This course examines the structural factors that led to the weakening of the Soviet Union in the 1970s and 1980s; its last leader, Mikhail Gorbachev's attempts to reinvigorate his country and its communist system through his policies of perestroika and glasnost'; how these reforms engendered the collapse of the Berlin Wall and the USSR; the creation of the modern Russian regime under Boris Yeltsin, whose presidency witnessed unprecedented corruption, kleptocracy, staggering inflation, and the emergence of the Russian mafiya; and the transition of power to Vladimir Putin. We conduct a deep dive into Putin's attempts to “make Russia great again” by embracing the tactics of his security state (KGB) roots and reasserting control over territories that had formerly belonged to the Russian Empire and the Soviet Union. We examine Putin's crackdown on the free press; civil rights; civil society/NGOs, and the wars he unleashed on Chechnya, Georgia, and Ukraine. We examine the evolution of youth culture; the position of women, members of the LGBT community, and non- Russian ethnic groups; the rise of the right-wing; climate change, and environmental problems related to Russia's fossil-fuel-based mono- economy; and topics of geopolitical and economic significance to the US government and its allies.Same as GOV/HIS/RUS319.

title: International Business
description: Students in this course will learn about the history of international business, investigate the political and economic institutions that structure the global economy, and explore the impact of international environments on firm-level decisions. Same as BOS 350.

title: Elementary Italian II
description: Continuation of ITA 101. Prerequisite: ITA 101 or placement.

title: Elementary Italian II
description: Continuation of ITA 101. Prerequisite: ITA 101 or placement.

title: Inter Italian Lang & Cult II
description: This course is the continuation of Italian 201 and as such is an intermediate-level language course whose aim is the continued development of listening, speaking, reading and writing skills, as well as a deepened understanding of contemporary Italian culture. It is also a transition course, designed to prepare students for advanced study in Italian language, literature and film. Prerequisite: ITA 201 or placement.

title: Elementary Japanese II
description: Continued practice in listening, speaking, reading, and writing skills of contemporary Japanese in cultural context. Further development of reading and writing Kanji characters. Prerequisite: JPN101 or permission of the instructor.

title: Intermediate Japanese II
description: Continued development of contemporary Japanese listening, speaking, reading, and writing skills at the intermediate level in cultural context, including handling a variety of informal and formal situations. Further practice in reading and writing Kanji characters. Prerequisite: JPN201 or permission of the instructor.

title: Intro to Japanese Pop Culture
description: Japan’s pop culture has gained great popularity all over the world. Such genres include Godzilla, anime, manga and J-pop, to name a few. This course examines several major genres focusing on historical and cultural background, and their impact on Japanese society. Through reading the writings of notable cultural critics, students will learn to analyze each genre in depth as well as examine the interrelationships among them. Each student will choose his/her own research topic for a final presentation.

title: Elem Modern Hebrew I
description: Introduction to the basic structures and vocabulary of Modern Hebrew, oral and written.

title: Judaism
description: This course delves into the study of Judaism as text and as a living, evolving practice. Students will read primary scriptural sources as well as foundational works of Jewish philosophy and mysticism. The dynamic interaction between Jewish text and ritual expression will be examined as students encounter Jewish themes of exile, peoplehood, holiness, and tikkun olam (world-fixing) across historical time periods and in a variety of Jewish cultural contexts. All students are welcome regardless of previous experience/knowledge of Judaism! Same as RST112.

title: Religion and the Senses
description: The blast of a shofar, the taste of a communion wafer, the call to prayer at dawn: for many believers, religion is encountered through the body before it is understood as an idea. Examining Judaism, Christianity, and Islam comparatively, this course devotes a unit to each of the five senses, considering how these traditions have cultivated ways of hearing, seeing, smelling, tasting, and touching the divine, and where they have drawn the line between devotion and excess. The course begins with scripture and its interpretive traditions, from the thunder and lightning at Sinai to the hallowing and burning of incense. It then turns to cities from the medieval period to the present, where communities of faiths have shared streets and soundscapes, and where many of these practices endure today.

title: Antisemitism & Visual Culture
description: Many of the most enduring anti-Jewish images were carved into the stone of medieval churches, and they remain there today. This course follows those images and their descendants from medieval sculpture and manuscripts through Nazi propaganda, political cartoons, and social media, paying close attention to how buildings and cities have marked Jews as outsiders. Students will learn to trace a motif across centuries, separating real lines of descent from coincidental resemblance, and will apply these tools to contested contemporary cases, including images connected to Israel, where scholars disagree about where criticism and satire end and antisemitism begins. Same as HAA174.

title: Elementary Latin II
description: LAT 102 continues and completes the study of the basic grammar and syntax of classical Latin. Prerequisite: LAT 101 or placement.

title: Intro to Latin Poetry
description: Introduction to Latin poetry with the goal of developing speed and facility in meter and interpretation. Prerequisite: LAT 201 or placement. Offered every Spring.

title: Latin Love Poetry
description: Passion, scandal, and bad romances: welcome to the world of Latin love poetry! We will read and translate a selection of love poems written by Roman authors such as Catullus, Ovid, Propertius, and the female poet, Sulpicia. Think modern dating is full of red flags? Wait until you meet the Romans! Prerequisite LAT 202 or permission.

title: Sociolinguistics
description: An exploration of the relationship between language, culture and society. Special attention will be paid to language variation (styling and codes, dialects, creoles and pidgins) and language in society (multilingualism, language prejudice, identities). Readings, films, discussions and group work will prepare students for field work. Please note that this Spring Offering will include a community component.

title: Psycholinguistics
prereq: LIN 101 OR PSY 100 OR PERMISSION OR SPM 100
description: This course explores language in the mind and brain, including: How do children learn their first language(s) and why is it such a different experience for an adult to learn a language? What are language disorders? Is spoken language processed differently from written language? What about sign languages? Class will include discussions, presentations, and hands-on analysis of language data. Prerequisite: LIN 101 or PSY 100 or SPM 100. Same as PSY 207.

title: Reading Beyond Borders
description: This course focuses on the three main themes of the Reckoning with Lancaster initiative – indigeneity, abolition, and migration – exploring their construction and deconstruction in narrative texts from various literary traditions from around the world. We will read novels and short stories by European writers of migrant background; works by former prisoners of various carceral systems; and narratives by indigenous writers from different areas of the world. We will address the following questions: How do these texts challenge existing cultural, linguistic, and national boundaries? How do they help us imagine a different, freer way on being and moving in the world?

title: Classical Myth
description: Introduction to the myths of ancient Greece and Rome and their relationship to the art, history, philosophy and religions of their respective cultures. Students will explore the Classical conception of the interactions between mortals, heroes and divinities through a wide range of media and textual genres. Connections between Greek and Roman myths as well as the adaption of mythical traditions from Near East cultures will be discussed. Same as CLS230.

title: Epic and Romance
description: This course focuses on epic and romance: two genres of ancient literature which mutually inform and influence each other, and both of which formulate the foundations and inspirations of popular 21st-century genres of fiction (fantasy, science fiction, romance, among others). Readings will be selected from texts including Homer’s Iliad and Odyssey, the Irish Táin Bó Cúailnge (The Cattle Raid of Cooley), Beowulf, the Arthurian romances of Chrétien de Troyes, Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, and Geoffrey Chaucer’s Troilus and Criseyde. Our discussions will focus on the formation of the notion of heroism, and examine various stages in the development of concepts of heroism in western culture, and the cultural fantasies that accompany it. Above all, epic and romance concern themselves with the process and problematics of selfdefinition, that of the individual and of the community as a whole. The course addresses the following questions: How was reading used as a method of unifying culture in secular communities? In what ways did these narratives affirm and/or challenge societal rules? How does this literature treat figures of the nation and the king? The conventions of gender? Same as ENG 253.

title: Indig/Colonial Entanglements
description: Whereas Indigenous peoples are marginalized in traditional accounts of US literature and history, this course foregrounds the textual legacy of the early, often violent entanglement of Native and colonial people. How did Indigenous writers represent themselves and their nations, and how did they recount and resist colonialism and genocide? How did encounters with Native people lead colonial, European, and US writers to see the world differently? We will read a wide variety of genres, some traditionally “literary” (memoirs, plays, fiction), some less so (colonial sales pitches, treaties, transcribed oratory). We’ll read texts with close attention to how they use language and how they frame Indigeneity, colonialism, cultural difference, and more. Fulfills the pre-1800 requirement for the English major. Same as ENG371.

title: Contemporary Indian Literature
description: Although fiction by Indians writing in English since the 1980s is probably best known on the world stage, Indians have been prolific producers of literature in English in a variety of genres for the last two centuries. Through exposure to fiction, poetry, and non-fiction, this course will offer a taste of the tremendous energy and vitality which characterizes literary production in India today. Students will also develop a picture of the fraught place English has occupied in India from the pre-Independence period to the first decade of this century. Meets 400-level seminar requirement for the English major or the contemporary literature requirement for majors in the creative writing track, or fulfills the NW or WP requirement. The course cannot count for more than one of the English major requirements. Permission of the instructor is required. Same as ENG494

title: Introduction to Data Science
prereq: MAT 109 OR MAT 110 OR MAT 111 OR CPS 111 OR PLACEMENT IN 112 OR CPS 173
description: The course introduces students to the foundations of data science. The examined topics include getting, wrangling, exploring, displaying and drawing conclusions from the data. Data ethics issues are also addressed. Data sets and examples are drawn from a wide variety of fields. The statistical program R is extensively used in this course to carry out all aspects of work with data. Prerequisite: MAT 109 or MAT 110 or MAT 111 or CPS 111 or CPS 173. Same as DSC 115.

title: Intro to Higher Mathematics
description: A course designed as a transition from calculus to advanced mathematics courses. Emphasis on discovering and writing proofs. Topics at instructor’s discretion. Examples: number theory, combinatorics and graph theory, discrete mathematics, mathematical analysis (including dynamical systems). Prerequisite: MAT110 or permission.

title: Intro to Statistical Modeling
prereq: MAT 109 OR MAT 110 OR MAT 111 OR PLACEMENT IN 110 OR PLACEMENT IN 111
description: This course is about the construction, analysis, and application of statistical models to real data. We emphasize the use of models to untangle and quantify variation in observed data. Basic statistical concepts such as randomness, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, causal inference, etc., are explored in the context of statistical models which include multivariate regression, analysis of variance, and logistic regression. We use a modern statistics software package (R) throughout the course. Prerequisite: MAT109. Same as DSC 215.

title: Probability and Statistics I
description: Introduction to single variable probability and statistics. Random variables. Binomial, geometric, Poisson, exponential and gamma distributions, among others. Counting techniques. Estimation and hypothesis tests on a single parameter. Prerequisite: MAT110.

title: Linear Algebra &Modrn Applicat
description: Linear Algebra is a foundation of modern pure and applied mathematics, data science, and machine learning. This course covers systems of linear equations and matrices, vector spaces, linear transformations, inner product spaces, determinants, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, orthogonality, least-squares approximations, and Markov chains. Additional topics may include the Principle Axes Theorem and singular value decomposition. Prerequisite: MAT110. Not available to students who have credit for MAT 229.

title: Probability and Statistics II
description: Continuation of MAT216. Multivariate distributions. Estimation and hypothesis tests for multiple parameters. Regression and correlation. Analysis of variance. Prerequisites: MAT111 & MAT216.

title: Introduction to Analysis
description: An introduction to the ideas and proof techniques specific to mathematical analysis. Real numbers, sequences, limits, derivatives, integrals, infinite series, cardinality; other topics as chosen by instructor. Prerequisite: MAT211.

title: CBL: Math for Optimization
description: Mathematical optimization techniques for solving real-world problems involving decision-making and resource allocation. Topics include linear, nonlinear, and discrete optimization (both constrained and unconstrained), duality, sensitivity analysis, and optimization under uncertainty. We cover applications to the natural and social sciences, including assignment, transportation, network flow, and gradient descent. Prerequisite: MAT111 and MAT229 or MAT230

title: Origami Math
description: An exploration of the many ways in which folding paper, or any stiff material, can be modeled mathematically, using geometry, combinatorics, linear algebra, and other areas. Emphasis will be on exploring physical models to make conjectures and then building a mathematical model to form proofs. In addition, recent applications of origami in engineering, physics, and the theory of computation will be covered. Pre-requisites: MAT211 and (MAT229 or MAT230) or permission of the instructor.

title: Time Series Analysis
description: Time series is a series of data points that were observed at different points in time. Observing the data at adjacent time points introduces correlation between observations. This correlation severely limits the use of the traditional statistical techniques due to their dependence on the usual assumption of independent and identically distributed observations. This course aims to provide a practical introduction to time series data analysis. The topics include model's identification, estimation, and assessment of suitability, modeling univariate time series data with ARIMA models, forecasting, regression models for time series data, etc.Pre-reqs: MAT/DSC215 and MAT216.

title: Shape of Space
description: We begin with the study of surfaces (2-dimensional universes)---classifying their shapes, understanding their geometries, and learning the beautiful connection between the two given by the Gauss-Bonnet Formula. Then, we move up a dimension to explore the mathematical possibilities for the shape and the geometry of our 3-dimensional universe. Time permitting, we will learn the cosmology needed to understand one approach to deciding amongst these possibilities. Pre-requisite: MAT330

title: Fundamentals
description: A first course in music for students with little or no formal training or background. Emphasis on basic musicianship including keyboard orientation, and the ability to read and sing simple melodies in treble and bass clefs, in both major and minor modes, and in a variety of meters. Additional topics include the notation of pitch and rhythm, scales, key signatures, time signatures, intervals, triads, and basic score navigation. No musical background required.

title: College Chorus
description: A large choral group of approximately 80 singers that concentrates on the masterpieces of the choral repertory, both a capella and with orchestra. Two rehearsals per week. Prerequisite: permission of the director.

title: Chamber Singers
description: A select vocal ensemble of 24 singers selected by audition. Repertory includes music from a wide range of musical styles and time periods. In addition to on-campus performances, the group embarks on annual tours. Two rehearsals per week. Prerequisite: Permission of the director.

title: Orchestra
description: A full orchestra with approximately 70 performers focusing on masterpieces of the orchestral repertoire. Two rehearsals per week. Prerequisite: Permission of the director.

title: Symphonic Wind Ensemble
description: A large ensemble for woodwinds, brass, and percussionists with approximately 50 performers. Repertory ranges from masterworks of the concert band tradition to new works written for wind ensemble. Two rehearsals per week. Prerequisite: Permission of the director.

title: Chamber Music
description: Chamber Music is designed for advanced instrumental music students to experience music written for generally 3 to 8 players. These small ensembles require high artistic demands on all of the ensemble members, as each player is essentially a soloist. Ensembles in this program rehearse a minimum of twice a week for a total of not less than 3 hours a week. One of the two rehearsals each week is coached by a professional chamber music coach. The ensemble is expected to perform on an appropriate concert at least once a semester. In the first semester of the course (156), the student will receive no credit. In the second semester of the course (256), the student will receive .5 credit.

The singer IS the instrument and must learn to play the instrument! Singing is a science. Singing is a mindful practice. It is a meditation. Singing is the expression of our personalities and our true selves.

title: Songwriting
description: An introduction to the art of songwriting. Students will create original lyrics and melodies and learn how to set them with suitable accompaniments. Topics covered will include aspects of sound, figures of speech, speaker perspective, rhyme, rhythm and meter, phrasing, chord progression, and form. Each student will compose and make recordings of two original songs with guidance and practical feedback from the instructor. A background in music performance and/or some experience with creative writing is strongly recommended. Same as ENG 205.

title: Anthropology of Music
description: Music can best be described as elusive. It is mobile and porous, traveling over space and time, interacting and melding with (sometimes rejecting) other musics it encounters. What music is to one people may be noise to another. Though its definition is culturally relative, what can be said about all music is that it does. Music functions differently from culture to culture and engaging with those functions not only aids in a deeper understanding of the music itself, but of the societies that produce them. This class will serve not only as an exploration of how music functions in various societal and cultural contexts, but how, through the practices of fieldwork and ethnography, these questions have been approached by scholars in the past (and the ethical implications of such work). Readings will be structured around case studies from minoritized, indigenous, diasporic/exilic, and post-colonial populations so as to allow us to move beyond commonly-held conceptions and understandings of music and dive into its too often unrecognized expanses. Same as ANT220.

title: Musicianship II

title: HipHop: Globl Poltcs of Cultur
description: Who gets to be "real" in hip hop? Why does being "real" matter? This course examines hip hop's "politics of authenticity," which opens avenues to help us speak about colonialism, white supremacy, sexism, and Black cultural resistance. Rightfully centering and honoring the genre's Afro-diasporic influences, we will examine debates involving transnationalism, gender, sexual, and racial boundaries in hip hop. We will also explore hip hop's global relevance, such as its sonic and cultural presence in reggaetón and its spread as a global dance form. Overall, this class will prompt students to untangle hip hop's seemingly contradictory ethos of "keeping it real" while simultaneously promoting broader ideals of cosmopolitanism and global commodification. Same as AFS/AMS/TND/WGS 239.

title: Conducting
description: This course will develop the following conducting skills: score study techniques, conducting gestures, rehearsal strategies, as well as aural discrimination and interpersonal skills. Class members will begin with basic movement exercises and work up to conducting a symphony orchestra in a rehearsal setting. The ability to read music in both treble and bass clefs is required, as is a basic knowledge of music theory with respect to key signatures (both major and minor), time signatures (both simple and compound), and basic chord progressions. Permission of the director required.

description: A large choral group of approximately 80 singers that concentrates on the masterpieces of the choral repertory, both a capella and with orchestra. Two rehearsals per week. Prerequisite: permission of the director.

description: A select vocal ensemble of 24 singers selected by audition. Repertory includes music from a wide range of musical styles and time periods. In addition to on-campus performances, the group embarks on annual tours. Two rehearsals per week. Prerequisite: Permission of the director.
