title: Chamber Music
description: Chamber Music is designed for advanced instrumental music students to experience music written for generally 3 to 8 players. These small ensembles require high artistic demands on all of the ensemble members, as each player is essentially a soloist. Ensembles in this program rehearse a minimum of twice a week for a total of not less than 3 hours a week. One of the two rehearsals each week is coached by a professional chamber music coach. The ensemble is expected to perform on an appropriate concert at least once a semester. In the first semester of the course (156), the student will receive no credit. In the second semester of the course (256), the student will receive .5 credit.

title: The Genius of Improvisation
description: Principles of jazz harmony and their application in improvisational practice. Emphasis on approaches to improvisation developed by revolutionary jazz artists, including Charlie Parker, Bud Powell, Miles Davis, and John Coltrane. Students will learn and practice material based on the techniques and devices set forth by these American innovators. Ability to read music and competence on a musical instrument (including voice) required. Prerequisite: MUS 100, 200, or permission of the instructor.

title: Music in the 19th Century
description: From Carnegie Hall to the Paris Opera to Classic FM, much of today’s “classical” music dates from the nineteenth century. How can we account for this music’s expressive power and enduring impact? In this class we will examine a wide range of nineteenth-century music by such composers as Ludvig van Beethoven, Franz Schubert, Frédéric Chopin, Clara and Robert Schumann, Giuseppe Verdi, Richard Wagner, and Peter Ilyich Tchaikovsky. Throughout, we will consider aspects of musical style, form, and expression in the context of the philosophical, literary, political, and social currents that informed these works. Prerequisite: ability to read music.

title: Song Cycles & Concept Albums
description: From Beethoven to Beyoncé, musicians have been organizing their work into collections of songs for more than two hundred years. These collections tell stories and explore themes, and they often provide windows into how subjective experiences and transformations have been understood and expressed in various historical contexts. This course explores the related genres of song cycles and concept albums from the early 1800s through the present day. In addition to Beethoven and Beyoncé, we will look at examples by Franz Schubert, Robert Schumann, Joni Mitchell, Marvin Gaye, Pink Floyd, and others. Throughout, the emphasis will be on the relationship between music and text, and the complex interactions between works of music and their cultural, social, and political contexts. The ability to read music is required for this course.

title: Water, Life & Society
description: This course examines the history, development, management, and policy issues associated with one of the most remarkable substances on Earth, water. The storage and flow of water in the natural world are explored to provide a basis for considering how people have rerouted water since the development of agriculture. The association between civilization and the construction of dams and irrigation projects is explored using case studies that include water conflicts and shortages from around the world. As population and consumption grow and water becomes increasingly scarce and/or polluted, water management and policy become more complex.

title: History of Medicine
description: The history of medicine with particular attention to American medicine. The relationship between medicine and society is studied in its historical context. We look in detail at some trends in modern medicine and the current debate over national health care policy in light of the history of medicine. Same as HIS/STS 311.

title: Occult Science & Pseudoscience
description: The class will gain a basic familiarity with the history of the occult sciences and pseudoscience. Students will learn about the boundaries between what they define as "bunk" and what they dub "legitimate" science, what is authentic knowledge about nature, and who gets to define what counts as proper science. Likewise, the class will gain skills to understand the nature of science itself and how it operates. Same as STS 365.

title: Narratives of Disability
description: Disability is a fundamental component of human diversity. We possess auditory and visual capacities in varying degrees, our minds process information differently, and we adapt to barriers in physical space in various manners. Due to illness, accidents, or aging, we undergo numerous types of temporary or permanent disability over the course of our lives. However, disability is not merely an embodied condition; it is also an experience shaped by social categories such as class, race, ethnicity, gender, sexuality, and able-bodiedness. How can we, then, define disability in a more stable sense? Which bodily and mental differences are considered inconsequential? Which are stigmatized? This course explores how we value some bodies and minds and devalue others, as well as how we embrace or resist notions of 'normal' behavior, fitness, and appearance. Same as STS/WGS 222.

title: Intro to Public Health
description: An introduction to public health, a field that endeavors to improve the health of populations through community-based action. The history of public health, how to measure population health, communicable diseases, chronic diseases, social determinants of health, family health, nutrition and food safety, environmental health, the U.S. national health care system, underserved groups, public health ethics, and the future of public health. Same as BIO/PUB/STS 251.

title: Epidemiology
description: Epidemiology is the study of health and disease of populations. In this course, students will learn methods epidemiologists use to elucidate relationships between various types of exposures and positive or negative health outcomes; they will also explore methods to trace and predict disease patterns, including epidemics and pandemics, and emphasizing SARS-CoV-2. In this course, students will learn how to develop research questions, design ethical studies, conduct sampling for research, perform basic analyses, and minimize bias and other types of error. Same as BIO354. Prerequisites: PBH251 or permission of instructor.

title: Race, Ethnicity, and Health
description: The course will utilize a sociological lens to examine the role of race and ethnicity in health outcomes, healthcare experiences, medical research, and clinical practice. Topics will include: socio-historical perspectives on notions of race in relation to biological difference; socio-historical understandings of the health consequences of racialized public health policies and politically sanctioned medical practices;contemporary racial and ethnic disparities in disease morbidity and mortality indicators; the operationalization of racial categories in epidemiological, public health, and biomedical research and practice; contemporary debates regarding race and genomics; and understandings of racial and ethnic dynamics in relation to health and medicine at the intersections of socioeconomic class, immigration status, gender, sexuality, and other markers of social identity. Same as AFS/SOC 366.

title: Social Inequality and Health
description: This course will use a sociological lens to examine how social inequality shapes health patterns, behaviors, and outcomes. We will explore the role of social and structural determinants of health, including race, immigration status, gender, education, occupation, families, social networks, and neighborhoods. We will also discuss clinical, policy, and other social interventions aimed at reducing health inequalities. This course is largely U.S.-focused, however many concepts and theories discussed can be applied in global settings. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or PBH 251. Same as SOC/STS 367.

title: Health Policy
description: This course investigates domestic and global health policy issues. We will survey health care and health systems, focusing on health care spending, insurance, and health outcomes. Students will also examine ethical dilemmas and debates within health policy. We will ask what role health policy can play in addressing health disparities. Two questions infuse our deliberations: what can the government do to shape the health of individuals and what should it do? Formerly PBH 410. Same as GOV 380.

title: PHR: Tobacco,Nicotine&ECigs
prereq: (PBH 354 OR BIO 354 ) AND (BIO 210 OR MAT 216 OR BOS 250 OR PSY 300 OR PSY 230 )
description: In this interdisciplinary seminar, students explore the epidemiology of tobacco use, related public health costs, and tobacco regulation. Students will navigate scientific literature on tobacco to develop hypotheses about the relationships between economic, behavioral, biological, sociopolitical, cultural, and environmental variables that influence prevention, dependence, and treatment. Students will design and conduct research centered on tobacco, nicotine, or e-cigarettes with an eye towards the policy implications of their work. Prerequisites: PBH 354, and one course from BIO 210, MAT 216, BOS 250, or PSY 300, or permission of the instructor.

title: Public Health Practice Seminar
prereq: BIO 354 OR PBH 354 OR GOV 380 OR PBH 380 OR PBH 473 OR PBH 474 OR STS 474
description: This seminar for advanced public health students will combine classroom and field work to explore various areas of public health practice. A service-learning model will be used, with focus on student learning, engagement with community needs and priorities, and critical reflection. Students will read about and discuss common themes in public health practice and spend approximately 8-10 hours weekly at a community-based site. Projects will be relevant to community health and involve at least one of several professional activities (e.g. assessment, programming, evaluation, education). Prerequisites: (BIO354 or PBH 354) OR (GOV380 or PBH380) OR (PBH473 or PBH474 or STS474).

description: Traditional philosophical problems of method, knowledge, the nature of reality, religious belief, and ethics.

title: Good Reasons
description: We aim to have good reasons for the beliefs we have and the decisions we make. Our class is about acquiring skills to accomplish this goal. We draw from a wide array of disciplines (including philosophy, cognitive psychology, behavioral economics, and decision theory) to address questions such as: What kinds of mental processes are involved in reasoning? What makes a line of reasoning valid or strong? Why do people tend to become more certain of the views they started with? Are there strategies we can use to avoid common errors in reasoning? What is evidence, and how does it interact with our background knowledge? What are the features of a community that respects good reasons?

title: Topics in AI and Philosophy
description: This course primarily explores what it means to be a good thinker in the context of artificial intelligence, bringing classic issues in the study of knowledge in contact with the challenges presented by AI. We also consider the distinction between the real and the fake, what makes a string symbols or sounds meaningful, and whether AI requires a radical change how we understand agency.

title: Moral Theory
description: A careful study of classic texts in moral philosophy, with an emphasis on questions about the foundations of ethics and the objectivity of moral judgement.

title: Language, Knowledge & Reality
description: This class is an advanced, but accessible, introduction to two central branches of philosophy: epistemology and metaphysics. Epistemology, loosely characterized, is the study of knowledge, evidence, and rationality. Metaphysics, even more loosely characterized, is the study of the general features of reality. We’ll work through some of the central topics that fall under these two studies, paying careful attention to how foundational questions about the nature of language interact with questions in epistemology and metaphysics.

title: Philosophy of Mind
prereq: One PHI or one PSY course
description: A general introduction to the philosophy of mind, addressing four key philosophical issues: the nature of psychological explanation, the mind-body problem, the possibility of artificial intelligence, and the nature of persons. Prerequisite: one course in philosophy or psychology. Prerequisite: One philosophy or one psychology course or permission of instructor.

title: Political Philosophy
description: This course is an introduction to political philosophy, with a focus on contemporary literature, questions, and issues. We’ll start by thinking about how to understand the basic concepts at the heart of political philosophy: rights, liberty, equality, autonomy, and justice. We’ll then shift to thinking about how these concepts play out in broader contemporary debates in political philosophy. These may include: political liberalism (and its critics), democracy, the justification of the state, anarchism, civil disobedience, distribution of goods, war, immigration, polarization, or political epistemology.

title: Current Work in Philosophy
description: This course directly engages students in the collective practice of doing philosophy while introducing them to current philosophical research. We will bring leading scholars to campus with each scholar delivering a public lecture, followed by a small colloquium or workshop that brings students directly into conversation with the visitor. Prior to each visit, we will cover readings related to the scholar’s current research and have a discussion session to prepare for entering the conversation with the scholar. Prerequisite: 2 prior philosophy classes. This course is graded Pass/No Pass. One half credit.

title: 20th Century Continental Phil
description: Close examination of emergence of modern phenomenology and hermeneutics. with particular attention to Heidegger’s Being and Time. Prerequisite: one prior course in philosophy or permission of the instructor.

title: Respect, Responsibility&Ethics
description: Recently many philosophers have argued that certain interpersonal emotions, such as resentment, indignation, guilt, gratitude, and approbation, are fundamental to a host of interconnected issues in ethics, including the nature of respect, dignity, freedom and responsibility, and the origins of moral values. This class will closely examine these claims and arguments with the aim of understanding more clearly how moral psychology and metaethics intersect. Prerequisite: one prior philosophy course.

title: Fem Phil of Cognitive Science
prereq: WGS 210 AND (PHI 100 OR PHI 130 OR PHI 236 OR PHI 250 OR PSY 100 OR PERMISSION OR PSY 203 OR SPM 100 OR STS 136 )
description: This course considers feminist perspectives and projects within or in response to philosophy of mind, cognitive neuroscience, and cognitive science. What can we meaningfully say about “the mind,” “the brain,” “the body,” “gender,” “experience,” “perception,” or “identity” without considering insights from each? Or without interrogating who the “we” is that pronounces these ultimate truths of the human condition? In pursuing the potential relationship between these fields we develop interdisciplinary and critical thinking skills needed to improve our understanding of human cognition in the context of uneven and oppressive material, social, and political realities. One focus will be on the significance of intersectionality for newer movements both in feminist thinking and in cognitive science. Same as PSY/WGS372. Pre-reqs: WGS210 and (PHI100 or PHI130 or PHI236 or PHI250 or PSY100 or PSY203 or SPM100 or STS136) or permission of the instructor.

title: Process and Product
description: The course is concerned the process/product distinction from the perspectives of both metaphysics and the philosophy of language. We will also be concerned how the metaphysics of this distinction has been used by recent authors to provide new perspectives on how to live a more meaningful life.

prereq: PHY 111 AND (MAT 229 (MAY BE TAKEN CONCURRENTLY) OR MAT 230 (MAY BE TAKEN CONCURRENTLY) )
description: Newton's laws applied to particles: rectilinear motion; simple, damped, and driven oscillations; gravitation and central forces; Lagrange's equations and the Hamiltonian; non-inertial frames of reference; and dynamics systems of particles. Laboratory work with computational modeling. Prerequisite: PHY 111. Corequisite: MAT 230 or MAT 229.

title: Expermntl Design & Communicatn
description: Physics is inherently an experimental science, so progress in physics relies on experiments to observe physical phenomena and test theoretical models. This course introduces several advanced practices in experimental physics. While many of these practices are technical (measurement design, instrumentation, data and uncertainty analysis), others are social (collaboration, communication, and ethical practice of science). The principles of experimental work are essential not only for further work in experimental science, but to guide theoretical and computational work in science. Prerequisite: PHY 223.

title: Quantum Mechanics
description: Basic postulates of quantum mechanics; wave equation in one and three dimensions; nondegenerate, degenerate, and time-dependent perturbation theory; the hydrogen atom. Prerequisite: PHY 223 and (PHY 331 or PHY 333).

description: An experimental and conceptual analysis of the processes of learning, thinking, and perception, and the biological bases of behavior. The relationships of these to behavioral development, social behavior, and more complex phenomena of personality formation and abnormal behavior is undertaken. Students cannot earn credit for both PSY 100 and PSY 101 unless permission is obtained from the department. Students enrolled in this course will be required to attend the Department's Bi-Annual Research Symposium held during the last week of classes.

title: Developmental Psychology
description: An examination of the relative contributions of nature and nurture on children's behavioral, cognitive, and perceptual development from the prenatal period through adolescence. Topics include the development of language, concepts, intelligence, socialization, motor abilities, and emotional understanding, with discussion informed by current and classic primary reading. Research activities and analyses integrated into course work. Prerequisite: PSY100 or SPM100. Previously PSY 304.

title: Health Psychology
prereq: (PSY 100 OR PERMISSION ) OR (BIO 101 OR BIOP FOR MIN. SCORE OF Y) OR SPM 100
description: This course explores the complex factors that affect human health, specifically examining how health and health-related behavior is influenced by the interrelationship of multiple environmental and individual factors ranging from individual personality to health policy. This course also examines the fundamental principles and theories of Health Psychology and how theoretical and empirical findings are applied to improve the health of individuals and groups. Prerequisite: PSY 100 or SPM 100 or BIO 101/110. Same as PBH 205. Previously PSY 317.

title: Psycholinguistics
prereq: LIN 101 OR PSY 100 OR PERMISSION OR SPM 100
description: This course explores language in the mind and brain, including: How do children learn their first language(s) and why is it such a different experience for an adult to learn a language? What are language disorders? Is spoken language processed differently from written language? What about sign languages? Class will include discussions, presentations, and hands-on analysis of language data. Prerequisite: LIN 101 or PSY 100 or SPM 100. Same as LIN 207.

title: Psychopathology
description: This course will serve as an introduction to descriptive and theoretical approaches to the study of psychopathology. In addition to the study of disease-related processes, special emphasis will be placed upon developing an understanding of those biological, psychological and social conditions that are essential for healthy psychosocial functioning across the life span. Prerequisite: PSY 100 or SPM 100 or permission. Previously PSY 308.

title: Hormones and Behavior
prereq: PSY 100 OR PERMISSION OR BIO 101 OR BIOP FOR MIN. SCORE OF Y
description: In this Biological Perspectives course, we’ll explore the role of hormones in three key areas of behavior: stress responses, sex, and relationships. How do hormones enable, regulate, or modify behavior in these contexts? How do behavior and the environment in turn affect hormone function? We’ll compare and contrast key theoretical models of hormones’ organization and activation effects based on human and animal studies to help us better understand our own behavior and give us insights into how culture and identity shape the kinds of research scientists pursue. Same as WGS237. Prerequisite: PSY100 or BIO101.

title: Psychology of Ideology
description: How do we form and maintain our belief systems? What would it take to change our minds about religion, politics, or morality? This discussion-based course will draw from a wide range of empirical research to illuminate how commitments to particular values and identities shape ideological thinking. We will investigate the sources of dogmatism and belief polarization, and we will explore how cognitive science can help us escape from echo chambers. Pre-reqs: PSY100 or SPM100 or permission of the instructor

title: Research Design and Statistics
prereq: (PSY 100 OR PERMISSION ) OR (BIO 101 OR BIOP FOR MIN. SCORE OF Y) OR SPM 100
description: This course will familiarize students with common research designs and statistical procedures used in psychology, primarily correlation and group difference designs. Class meetings focus on ethically describing, analyzing, and interpreting data, while labs help build your research design, teamwork, implementation, and presentation skills. When you complete this course, you should have the knowledge to think critically about the results of research you encounter in your everyday life and the skills to perform scientific studies of your own. Offered every semester. Prerequisites: PSY 100 or BIO 101/110 or SPM 100. Permission required. Previously PSY 230.

title: Animal Behavior w/Lab
prereq: (BIO 101 OR PERMISSION ) AND (PSY 300 (MAY BE TAKEN CONCURRENTLY) OR PSY 230 (MAY BE TAKEN CONCURRENTLY) OR BIO 210 (MAY BE TAKEN CONCURRENTLY) )
description: An integrative approach to animal behavior from the perspectives of ethology, behavioral ecology, and comparative psychology. We will explore the structure, function, development, and evolution of behavioral adaptations including orientation, foraging and predation, communication, social organization, and reproductive strategies. We will also discuss concepts particularly relevant to the modern world, including animal behavior pertaining to conservation, climate change, and interactions with humans. This course will include both lecture and lab components, and require individual and group project work.. Prerequisites: BIO 101, and permission of instructor. Corequisites: BIO 210 or PSY 300/230, and permission of the instructor. Same as BFB/BIO 320. Previously PSY 250.

title: Psychopharmacology w/Lab
prereq: (PSY 100 OR PERMISSION OR BIO 101 OR BIOP FOR MIN. SCORE OF Y OR SPM 100 ) AND (PSY 300 OR PSY 230 OR BIO 210 )
description: This 300-level course examines the effects of psychoactive drugs on brain function and behavior across multiple species. Students will explore neurotransmission, concepts of addiction, and the history of pharmacotherapy. Key topics include the pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics of both medicinal treatments and misused drugs. The course also examines the sociocultural influences of drugs on society, providing a foundation for students pursuing careers in psychology, neuroscience, or public health. Prerequisite: (PSY 100 or SPM 100 or BIO 101) AND (PSY 300 or BIO 210).

title: Cognitive Psychology w/Lab
description: Cognitive psychology examines how the human mind processes, interprets, and uses information. Although we often feel like experts on our own minds, research shows that mental processes are heavily influenced by interacting internal and external forces. This course introduces the core theories and research methods that form the foundation of cognitive psychology, through in class-exercises, empirical readings, and class discussion. The laboratory component provides hands-on experience designing, conducting, and analyzing cognitive research. Prerequisites: PSY100 and PSY300. Not available to students who have credit for PSY305.

title: Fem Phil of Cognitive Science
prereq: WGS 210 AND (PHI 100 OR PHI 130 OR PHI 236 OR PHI 250 OR PSY 100 OR PERMISSION OR PSY 203 OR SPM 100 OR STS 136 )
description: This course considers feminist perspectives and projects within or in response to philosophy of mind, cognitive neuroscience, and cognitive science. What can we meaningfully say about “the mind,” “the brain,” “the body,” “gender,” “experience,” “perception,” or “identity” without considering insights from each? Or without interrogating who the “we” is that pronounces these ultimate truths of the human condition? In pursuing the potential relationship between these fields we develop interdisciplinary and critical thinking skills needed to improve our understanding of human cognition in the context of uneven and oppressive material, social, and political realities. One focus will be on the significance of intersectionality for newer movements both in feminist thinking and in cognitive science. Same as PHI/WGS372. Pre-regs: WGS210 and (PHI100, or PHI130 or PHI250 or PSY100 or PSY203 or SPM100 or STS136) or permission of the instructor.

title: Cognitive Development
prereq: PSY 202 OR PSY 304 OR PSY 305 OR PSY 311
description: In a matter of months, a zygote goes from a collection of cells to a thinking, feeling, learning baby…who quickly goes on to be a walking, talking, problem-solving toddler…who soon after is a reading, writing, socially-aware child. It’s breathtaking! This advanced, discussion- focused seminar explores the foundations of cognitive processes and developmental mechanisms that underpin our fantastic human cognitive growth. As we survey major topics in cognitive development, our focus will be primarily on birth through early childhood, asking the question: How do infants and children make sense of the myriad people, ideas, and objects around them? Prerequisite: PSY 202/304 or PSY305 or PSY311.

title: CBL: Applied Psychol Science
description: In this course, you will learn how to apply findings from basic psychological research to solve realworld problems. Students will work in partnership with local community groups to select a realworld problem of interest to address and complete a project. Final projects will be presented to a panel of researchers and community members. The course is collaborative in nature; you will work in groups to design and conduct your research and much of your grade in this course will be groupbased. This course is for senior Psychology majors. Students are required to complete 3 hours per week of out-of-class time at their community partners' location

title: Collab Res:Animal Behv &Models
prereq: (PSY 300 OR PSY 230 OR BIO 210 ) AND (PSY 203 OR PSY 312 OR PSY 310 OR PSY 320 OR PSY 250 OR PSY 351 OR PSY 302 OR PSY 357 OR BIO 357 OR WGS 357 OR PSY 303 OR BIO 303 OR WGS 303 OR PSY 464 OR PSY 306 ) AND (PSY 320 OR PSY 250 OR PSY 351 OR PSY 302 OR PSY 352 OR PSY 354 OR PSY 355 OR PSY 356 OR PSY 357 OR BIO 357 OR WGS 357 OR PSY 358 OR PSY 303 OR BIO 303 OR WGS 303 )
description: Students will work in teams to generate a research question, design a study, earn institutional ethics approval, collect and analyze data, and disseminate their findings on questions focused on non-human animals. Projects may aim to better understand the animals themselves or use animals as models for human behavior. Research areas within this collaborative course may include any aspect of animal behavior in the field or in the laboratory. Research topics will reflect student interest and the expertise of the course instructor. Laboratory research required. Prerequisites: PSY 300/230 or BIO 210; and one of PSY 203/312, PSY 310, PSY 320/250, PSY 351/302, PSY 357/303, PSY 464/306; and one PSY lab course beyond PSY 300; or permission.

title: Collab Res Hum Behav Soc Evol
prereq: PSY 352 OR ( (PSY 201 OR PSY 315 OR PSY 204 OR PSY 319 OR PSY 206 OR PSY 307 OR PSY 309 ) AND (PSY 320 OR PSY 351 OR PSY 302 OR PSY 354 OR PSY 355 OR PSY 356 OR PSY 357 OR BIO 357 OR WGS 357 OR PSY 358 OR PSY 303 OR BIO 303 OR WGS 303 ) )
description: Students will work in research teams to generate a research question, design a study, collect and analyze data, and disseminate their findings. Research areas include experimental social psychology and/or evolutionary psychology. Research topics will reflect student interest and the expertise of the course instructor. Laboratory research required. Prerequisites: PSY352 OR one of PSY 201/315, PSY 204/319, PSY 206/307, PSY 309; and one PSY lab course beyond PSY 300; or permission.

title: Judaism
description: This course delves into the study of Judaism as text and as a living, evolving practice. Students will read primary scriptural sources as well as foundational works of Jewish philosophy and mysticism. The dynamic interaction between Jewish text and ritual expression will be examined as students encounter Jewish themes of exile, peoplehood, holiness, and tikkun olam (world-fixing) across historical time periods and in a variety of Jewish cultural contexts. All students are welcome regardless of previous experience/knowledge of Judaism! Same as JST112.

title: Islam
description: This course is an introduction to the intellectual and political history of Islam in both pre-modern and contemporary times. Several major aspects of Islamic religious thought will be covered including the Qur‘an and its interpretation, the persona and prophetic authority of Muhammad, law and theology, law and gender, Islamic mysticism, and contemporary Muslim reform movements. We will use a range of sources including primary religious texts (all in translation), anthropological works, novels, films etc. to examine the diversity and complexity of Muslim thought and practice, both past and present. While focusing on Islam, this course will also familiarize students with larger conceptual questions and problems in the academic study of religion.

title: Asian Religions
description: Historical and thematic survey of the major religious traditions of Asia, concentrating on the more influential traditions of India, China, Japan, and Tibet. Covers select traditions of ancient and modern forms of Hinduism, Buddhism, Confucianism, and Daoism. Focuses on doctrine, myth, and ritual in particular cultural and historical contexts.

title: Christian Nationalism in US
description: This course examines Christian nationalist ideology in the context of contemporary U.S. politics. Class readings and discussions will focus on Christian nationalism’s theological legitimizing narratives, social and cultural ambitions, nostalgic approach to history, and political impact.

title: Religion and Non-Violence
description: An investigation of the intersection of religion and violence, with specific focus on the challenges of nonviolence in various religious traditions. This is a discussion-oriented class in which students address nonviolent movements, protests, and approaches to violence that arise within various communities. We will review the lives, writings, and speeches of leaders like Mahatma Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr. and see how their work has affected religious groups and contemporary issues such as interplay between religion, nonviolence, language, and ecology. Students will apply what they have learned to particular ethical situations and dilemmas related to violence.

title: Psych of Religious Experience
description: An investigation of the psychological processes that involved in religious and spiritual experiences. A discussion-style format will link a psychological approach to religion to topics like worship, conversion, and death. Analysis of the formation and expression of religious experiences will be studied via foundational theorists and research approaches. Psychological focuses will be given to how sensation, perception and cognitive mechanisms (like biology, evolutionary, and moral reasoning) affect religious and spiritual experiences in the present day but also in history. This course will consider how cultural and social factors shape the development of spirituality, as well as how regulating emotion and behavior is expressed through religious experiences.

title: Relign,Death&Right to Die Mvmt
description: This class will examine legal, moral, and ethical events that have shaped American health care policy; students will discuss social values and obligations as exemplified in the systems we have built ostensibly to care for one another and protect human value. The class introduces and fosters critical thinking techniques and applies them to public policy, media literacy, language, and seemingly values- based government systems. It will encourage free-ranging exposure to texts and traditions and promote critical thinking and curiosity.

title: Religion and Film
description: How does religion look, feel, and sound on film? How do movies mediate and produce religious subjects? And what might we learn about religion and religion-making through attention to the particularities of cinema? This course looks at religion in film. More specifically, we examine religion and film with three different foci: (1) the representation of religion in cinema; (2) the formation of religious subjects through movies; (3) religion-making in the techniques, production, and distribution of film. We will approach film not only as a potent medium for the global circulation of religious traditions but also as a generative site for analyzing the sensorial and affective power of religion more broadly. Same as FLM 279.

title: Hindus and Muslims
description: This course will introduce students to the religious, legal, and political history and present of South Asia (the Indian sub-continent) by exploring the diversity of encounters between its two most populous religious communities: Hindus and Muslims. While critiquing nationalist histories that look at the relationship between these communities through the prism of either conflict or friendship, this course will develop a more nuanced picture of the critical traditions and moments of intra-religious and inter-religious discourses and debates that have shaped Hindu-Muslim relations in the last several centuries.

title: Artificial Intelligence & You
description: This course explores the following questions: What is intelligence? How do definitions, and experiences, of intelligence change over time? How do we understand the practices and tools of AI as products of historical and economic forces? How have commitments to military advantage inflected the science of so-called learning machines? And what does the rapid rise in the visibility and availability of artificial intelligence bode for you and all the other classified subjects in your midst? Same as STS 353.

title: Self, Society & Nature CHN JPN
description: A thematic exploration of self, society, nature, and their inter-relationships as conceived in Chinese and Japanese religions, especially Daoism, Buddhism, and Confucianism. Addresses these issues through translations of classical Chinese and Japanese texts, then examines how they play out in a number of historical periods, including the modern. We will end with some examples of recent East Asian concepts and practices embody certain themes in ancient traditions while adapting to the unique challenges of modernity.

title: Making Sense of Putin's Russia
description: This course examines the structural factors that led to the weakening of the Soviet Union in the 1970s and 1980s; its last leader, Mikhail Gorbachev's attempts to reinvigorate his country and its communist system through his policies of perestroika and glasnost'; how these reforms engendered the collapse of the Berlin Wall and the USSR; the creation of the modern Russian regime under Boris Yeltsin, whose presidency witnessed unprecedented corruption, kleptocracy, staggering inflation, and the emergence of the Russian mafiya; and the transition of power to Vladimir Putin. We conduct a deep dive into Putin's attempts to “make Russia great again” by embracing the tactics of his security state (KGB) roots and reasserting control over territories that had formerly belonged to the Russian Empire and the Soviet Union. We examine Putin's crackdown on the free press; civil rights; civil society/NGOs, and the wars he unleashed on Chechnya, Georgia, and Ukraine. We examine the evolution of youth culture; the position of women, members of the LGBT community, and non- Russian ethnic groups; the rise of the right-wing; climate change, and environmental problems related to Russia's fossil-fuel-based mono- economy; and topics of geopolitical and economic significance to the US government and its allies.Same as GOV/HIS/IST319.

title: Intro to Sociology
description: Introduction to the basic concepts, theories, and methods used to study human social interaction and social structures. Readings and topics vary section to section, but typically address social stratification (primarily by race, class, and gender) and its impact on individual and social life, the sources of social order and social change, deviance and social control, and the interrelations between individuals and society. Prerequisite to all other departmental offerings.

Prerequisite to all other departmental offerings.

title: Hist of Sociological Theory
prereq: SOC 100 plus one other SOC course
description: A critical examination of the development of social thought from the Enlightenment to the early Twentieth Century. The main focus is on past attempts to explain the nature of capitalism and its attendant transformation of family, work, and community. In addition, the course probes the question of how shared ideals and divisive interests affect both the internal coherence of human society and the study of human society as well. Prerequisites: SOC100 plus any other sociology course.

title: Power and Resistance
description: The nature of power has long been a central concern for political sociology. In this course we will analyze major political institutions and phenomena, including nationalism, state formation, domination and authority, resistance and social movements, civil society, and political change. Examples and case studies will be drawn from multiple countries, including Chile, Russia/USSR, the US, continental Europe, the Arab Spring movements of 2011, and elsewhere. Prerequisite: SOC 100.

title: Race and Ethnic Relations
description: The premise of this course is that the concept of “race” operates as a socio-historically situated construction to which social, political, and legal meanings are ascribed. We will be exploring the fluidity of racial categorization systems, with special attention to the deconstruction of “whiteness” as a consistently privileged, yet socio-historically malleable, category. Our readings and discussions will span dimensions of racialization in culture, media, political discourse, social movements, education, housing, and labor force participation. We will be using a variety of media to examine topics such as racial identity development processes, the evolution of white privilege, the social construction of racialized “otherness”, and the ways in which the institutionalization of racialized ideologies has resulted in the unequal distribution of power, material resources, and opportunities in the United States. Lastly, we will explore how racial identity categories intersect with other social identity categories such as gender, socio-economic class, citizenship, religion, and sexuality. Prerequisite: SOC 100. Same as AFS 360.

title: Race, Ethnicity, and Health
description: The course will utilize a sociological lens to examine the role of race and ethnicity in health outcomes, healthcare experiences, medical research, and clinical practice. Topics will include: socio-historical perspectives on notions of race in relation to biological difference; socio-historical understandings of the health consequences of racialized public health policies and politically sanctioned medical practices;contemporary racial and ethnic disparities in disease morbidity and mortality indicators; the operationalization of racial categories in epidemiological, public health, and biomedical research and practice; contemporary debates regarding race and genomics; and understandings of racial and ethnic dynamics in relation to health and medicine at the intersections of socioeconomic class, immigration status, gender, sexuality, and other markers of social identity. Same as AFS/PBH 366.

title: Social Inequality and Health
description: This course will use a sociological lens to examine how social inequality shapes health patterns, behaviors, and outcomes. We will explore the role of social and structural determinants of health, including race, immigration status, gender, education, occupation, families, social networks, and neighborhoods. We will also discuss clinical, policy, and other social interventions aimed at reducing health inequalities. This course is largely U.S.-focused, however many concepts and theories discussed can be applied in global settings. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or PBH 251. Same as PBH/STS 367.

title: The 21st Century Workplace
description: Work is a fundamental aspect of human life, and it has shaped society as we know it. In this course, we will study its various forms and dynamics: paid and unpaid work; formal and informal labor markets; the types of work individuals perform; their remuneration and conditions of work; as well as material and status inequalities. We will explore emerging forms of work, including large scale trends as well as micro-level dynamics of work and the meanings they generate in the lives of workers around the world and across various sectors of American society. This course will help students develop a complex understanding of the 21st century workplace by contextualizing it sociologically and interdisciplinarily. This class will help students situate their own past, current, and future work experiences within sociological frameworks. Prerequisite: SOC100

title: Marco/Frame
prereq: SPA 202 OR PLACEMENT IN ADVANCED LOW OR ADVANCED MID
description: Films and literature help us grasp global issues by framing them in individual stories. This course focuses on developing language and critical thinking skills in Spanish through the analysis of films and texts from the Hispanic world. By delving into their stories, characters and conflicts, and through conversations, presentations, essays and creative expression, we will explore the individual toll of large-scale problems such as human obsolescence, neoimperialism, and identity politics. Prerequisite: SPA 202 or placement into Advanced Low or Mid.

title: Caleidoscopio
prereq: SPA 202 OR PLACEMENT IN ADVANCED LOW OR ADVANCED MID
description: A kaleidoscope allows us to see multiple perspectives and stands as a symbol of the complexity of the human experience. This course aims at developing students’ linguistic and critical thinking abilities in Spanish by means of analyzing cultural artifacts from the Hispanic world with a focus on perspective. We will pay special attention to exploring our and other people’s points of view through empathy, imagination, and (self) reflection. We will also put emphasis on conversing and writing in Spanish as well as on experiential learning. Prerequisite: SPA 202 or placement into Advanced Low or Mid. Students who completed SPA 222A in Spring 2025 are not eligible to take this course.

title: Spanish Grammar
prereq: 2 COURSES AT 221-250 LEVEL; OR ADVANCED MID PLACEMENT AND 1 COURSE AT 221-250 LEVEL; OR PLACEMENT IN 321
description: An in-depth study of the more subtle nuances of Spanish grammar including narration in the past and the subjunctive with a strong emphasis on oral and written practice. The course includes reading about the grammatical system. If we have enough students, we will be doing a "Reacting to the Past Unit" involving the Phillips Museum. Prerequisite: Two courses at the 221-250 level; or Advanced Mid placement and one course at the 221-250 level; or placement into SPA 321.

title: Miradas críticas
prereq: 2 COURSES AT 221-250 LEVEL; OR ADVANCED MID PLACEMENT AND 1 COURSE AT 221-250 LEVEL; OR PLACEMENT IN 321
description: Spanish 321 emphasizes the appreciation, understanding and analysis of various types of literature, art, and popular culture. This course will introduce you to the methodologies used to interpret different cultural artifacts, including fiction, non-fiction and the visual arts. it will also help you to develop your analytical, interpretative and writing skills through a regular practice of close reading. We will discuss representative works from different historical periods from Spain and Latin America. We will also focus on the writing process and argumentation. In this way, the work that you do for this class will help prepare you for more advanced courses in Spanish and other disciplines. Prerequisite: Two courses at the 221-250 level; or Advanced Mid placement and one course at the 221-250 level; or placement into SPA 321.

title: España en pantalla
prereq: 2 COURSES AT 221-250 LEVEL; OR ADVANCED MID PLACEMENT AND 1 COURSE AT 221-250 LEVEL; OR PLACEMENT IN 321
description: 21st century Spain has very little to do with the country it was just a century ago, or has it? In this course, we will explore the cinematic representation of key historical events from the 20th century that continue to shape today’s Spanish society and culture. Through informed discussions of themes such as history, memory, violence, gender, and migration, and their depiction in movies, students will gain insight into Contemporary Spanish society. In addition, students will develop basic notions of cinematography and film analysis to help them speak and write critically about the themes depicted in the films. Prerequisites: (SPA 221 and SPA 222 ) OR (placement in ADVANCED MID and SPA 221 or 222) OR placement in 321

title: Mujeres nuevas, viejas ideas
description: This course analyzes the existing contradictions in the construction of femininity during the Spanish Second Republic and the Francoist dictatorship through a variety of texts, genres, and women authors. It pays special attention to education, children’s literature, and the figure of the female teacher, due to their relevance in gender construction. Prerequisite: SPA 321. Same as WGS 425

title: Minds, Machines, and Morals
description: This course provides an introduction to the central problems, concepts, and methods of cognitive science and moral psychology. We will analyze questions addressing the nature of intelligence, the relationship between minds and bodies, and the basis of moral beliefs and behaviors. These explorations will bridge the sciences and humanities by taking a fundamentally interdisciplinary perspective.

title: Environment and Human Values
description: Study of historical and modern attitudes toward nature; human use of nature's resources; the effects of the growth of science and technology on human uses of and attitudes toward the environment; and modern humans' ability to substantially alter the environment (e.g., by altering global temperature). Key concepts addressed include the nature of human population growth, the notion of "limits to growth," and the difficulty of managing the use of common pool resources. Same as ENE 117.

title: Environment and Human Values
description: Study of historical and modern attitudes toward nature; human use of nature's resources; the effects of the growth of science and technology on human uses of and attitudes toward the environment; and modern humans' ability to substantially alter the environment (e.g., by altering global temperature). Key concepts addressed include the nature of human population growth, the notion of "limits to growth," and the difficulty of managing the use of common pool resources. Same as ENE 117.

title: Narratives of Disability
description: Disability is a fundamental component of human diversity. We possess auditory and visual capacities in varying degrees, our minds process information differently, and we adapt to barriers in physical space in various manners. Due to illness, accidents, or aging, we undergo numerous types of temporary or permanent disability over the course of our lives. However, disability is not merely an embodied condition; it is also an experience shaped by social categories such as class, race, ethnicity, gender, sexuality, and able-bodiedness. How can we, then, define disability in a more stable sense? Which bodily and mental differences are considered inconsequential? Which are stigmatized? This course explores how we value some bodies and minds and devalue others, as well as how we embrace or resist notions of 'normal' behavior, fitness, and appearance. Same as PBH/WGS 222.

title: The Age of Enlightenment
description: "What is Enlightenment?" This question was posed by Immanuel Kant in 1784 and has intrigued historians since. Was the Enlightenment a unified body of thought? What was the goal of the "Enlightenment project"? How did it impact more than the history of ideas, to influence cultural practices and the daily lives? What was its relationship to contemporary political systems? This course will explore Enlightenment debates and developments. Topics for discussion will include the birth of the intellectual; the idea of the public sphere; religious enlightenment and secularism; race, slavery, and colonialism; the gender politics of the Enlightenment; Enlightenment and revolution; and the modern legacy of the Enlightenment. Same as HIS/FRN/WGS 224.

title: Indigenous Environmntl Justice
description: Examination of the way indigenous identity, human rights, and development intersect with the struggle for environmental justice around the world. Analysis of how each term in this course's title is open to legal fixing, activist redefinition, and diverse projects that render the environment something political. Considers distinct case studies drawn from several continents to show that some see being indigenous today as politically potent, while others take this category to be excessively vague or, even, invented; by focusing on ordinary lives and extraordinary struggles, we explore the wide variety of relationships to territory that "indigenous" encapsulates. Same as ANT/ENE 244.

title: History of Medicine
description: The history of medicine with particular attention to American medicine. The relationship between medicine and society is studied in its historical context. We look in detail at some trends in modern medicine and the current debate over national health care policy in light of the history of medicine. Same as HIS/NSP 311.

title: N. American Environ History
description: Examination of various approaches to American environmental and ecological history. Focuses on ways in which the physical and biological world have affected human history and on ways in which American social and political organizations, economic activities, cultural values and scientific theories have shaped Americans' interactions with nature. Selected case studies from American environmental history, with emphasis on the 17th through the 20th centuries. Same as HIS/ENE 312.

title: Artificial Intelligence & You
description: This course explores the following questions: What is intelligence? How do definitions, and experiences, of intelligence change over time? How do we understand the practices and tools of AI as products of historical and economic forces? How have commitments to military advantage inflected the science of so-called learning machines? And what does the rapid rise in the visibility and availability of artificial intelligence bode for you and all the other classified subjects in your midst? Same as RST 353.

title: Occult Science & Pseudoscience
description: The class will gain a basic familiarity with the history of the occult sciences and pseudoscience. Students will learn about the boundaries between what they define as "bunk" and what they dub "legitimate" science, what is authentic knowledge about nature, and who gets to define what counts as proper science. Likewise, the class will gain skills to understand the nature of science itself and how it operates. Same as NSP 365.

We will explore the role of social and structural determinants of health, including race, immigration status, gender, education, occupation, families, social networks, and neighborhoods. We will also discuss clinical, policy, and other social interventions aimed at reducing health inequalities. This course is largely U.S.-focused, however many concepts and theories discussed can be applied in global settings. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or PBH 251. Same as SOC/PBH 367.

title: Introduction to Ballet
description: Basic technique and theory of ballet, including the anatomical laws governing ballet movement and investigation of the style and aesthetic of ballet technique. The course emphasizes the practice of dancing as well as that of writing, thinking and speaking clearly about ballet. Not for students with extensive previous experience in ballet.

title: Hip Hop: Movement and Culture
description: Hip hop reveals how culture exists in the body, in movement, and how movement influences culture. In this course, students will learn not only through moving/dancing, but also through discussion, viewing, reading and writing, to gain understanding of the history of hip hop culture and related street dance forms including funk styles, breakin', hip hop social dance, and club dances.

title: Technical Theatre Practicum
description: This course is designed to provide students with experiential training in the practical aspects of theatre production. students will engage with production-specific arenas of technical theatre, which can include: carpentry, rigging, lighting/electrical work, audio production/set up, video production/set up, etc. Toward developing a solid understanding of technical areas of performance production, students will choose one of two tracks: Process (over the course of the semester) or Production (intensive, aligned with departmental curricular productions), each with equivalent hours. The course is offered only as P/NP. One half credit.

title: Production Studio I
description: Introductory performance work in theatre with research and analysis relevant to the given production, including the work of actors, assistant dramaturgs, assistant stage managers (.5 credit per semester; may be repeated for elective credit; offered each semester). Prerequisite: permission of the instructor.

title: Dance Company
description: Credit for work undertaken toward performance in at least two mainstage College productions in the course of one academic year. Students are cast in choreographies by audition. Rehearsal, Company class, and performance participation are mandatory. For TND 200, students receive no credit, but .5 credit is awarded with the completion of TND 201. Prerequisites: audition and permission of the instructor.

title: Dance Company
description: Credit for work undertaken toward performance in at least two mainstage College productions in the course of one academic year. Students are cast in choreographies by audition. Rehearsal, Company class, and performance participation are mandatory. For TND 200, students receive no credit, but .5 credit is awarded with the completion of TND 201. Prerequisites: audition and permission of the instructor.

title: Costume Design
description: The process of designing a costume from analyzing the script through the finished product. Examines the history of Western costume and other designers' work. Projects will allow students to apply theory, technique, and research in achieving their own designs. Same as ART 225.

title: HipHop: Globl Poltcs of Cultur
description: Who gets to be "real" in hip hop? Why does being "real" matter? This course examines hip hop's "politics of authenticity," which opens avenues to help us speak about colonialism, white supremacy, sexism, and Black cultural resistance. Rightfully centering and honoring the genre's Afro-diasporic influences, we will examine debates involving transnationalism, gender, sexual, and racial boundaries in hip hop. We will also explore hip hop's global relevance, such as its sonic and cultural presence in reggaetón and its spread as a global dance form. Overall, this class will prompt students to untangle hip hop's seemingly contradictory ethos of "keeping it real" while simultaneously promoting broader ideals of cosmopolitanism and global commodification. Same as AMS/AFS/MUS/WGS 239.

title: Modern & Contemp Amer Drama
description: A literary and theatrical examination of representative American Drama from the early twentieth century to the present, emphasizing developments since 1950. The focus of this study is on how and why Americans and American life have been depicted onstage as they have and the powerful effect this range of depictions has had on American identity and the American imagination. Same as AMS 251.

title: Digitl Renderng for Entertnmnt
description: Effectively rendering a spatial design can take many forms. Designers have long made use of physical models and perspective drawings to present and iterate design ideas as part of their process and to collaborate with other production staff. Modern computer aided design applications are able to utilize 3D environments to render realistic and physically accurate views and can work alongside other components of the design process. This course utilizes Blender, a free and open source 3D design software, to design environments for events such as theatrical performances, media installations, concerts, and corporate events. Students will gain an intermediate understanding of the program and how it can interact with other aspects of a design process through theoretical production situations and projects. Same as ART 270.

title: Student New Works Festival
description: Students participate as performers, technicians, stage managers, and more while working on this production-oriented course. Under the guidance of a faculty director, students engage in new play development processes as they take student-written work from page to stage. One half credit. Prerequisite: permission of the instructor.

title: Theatre for Social Change
description: This course examines how theatre can be used as a tool for social change and cultural reflection. Students will look at both historical and contemporary examples of theatrical social justice movements; from agitprop and documentary theatre to contemporary devised work. This course will examine how social justice movements have challenged institutional power and created space for marginalized voices. Through the analysis of text, readings, and participation with local organizations and advocacy work, this course will develop a framework for theatre as a political document and call to action. The course will culminate in a collaborative, semester-long project – in partnership with a faculty member or student organization – working towards a specific goal. Students will research, devise, and perform an original or adapted theatre piece that serves the partnership organization's mission. Same as AFS/WGS 272.

title: Embodying Ritual, Myth &Magick
description: This course explores the body as a site for ritual. Through the study of gesture, folkloric practice, choreography, improvisation and creative process we will look at how our bodies serve as vessels to embody the sacred other. We will cover a wide range of cultural practices to learn about embodiments of ancestral divination, seasonal rites aligned with solar and lunar cycles, ancestral divination, spectacle, possession and trance dance, animism, paganism and witchcraft. We will examine reconstructions of ancient practices as well as contemporary practices that emerge in response to socio-historical events. This is a studio-based dance course where movement will be a primary mode of learning.

title: Acting IId:Devised Performance
description: Devised theatre is an experimental collaborative acting course that introduces students to techniques, resources, and exploration in the theories and methodologies of devised theatre. Rather than starting with a script, students use improvisation, character development, and adaptation to create original performance work. Through critical analysis students will develop a working knowledge of how devised theatre is built from initial concept to final performance. This course culminates in a collaborative performance art project that demonstrates the creative and technical elements of the devising process.

title: Acting IIa: Shakespeare
description: Theory and practice of acting techniques focused on skills necessary to understand and perform Shakespeare's classical verse and action-based acting. Students will cultivate an understanding of their unique vocal and physical instrument. Audition techniques will be introduced. Prerequisite: TND186.

title: Hist of Western Theatre Dance
description: Survey of the historical, political and cultural forces that have shaped and influenced stage dancing in much of Western Europe and the Americas beginning with the renaissance and moving through the baroque, romantic, classical, modern and contemporary periods. Class formats include lecture, discussions and studio sessions.

title: Playwriting II
description: An upper level writing workshop, exploring advanced concepts and theories of writing for the stage. Students will complete the first draft of a full-length play. Prerequisite: TND 283 or instructor permission. Same as ENG 383.

title: Production Studio II
description: Combines performance work in theatre with research an analysis relevant to the given production, including the work of actors, assistant directors, assistant designers and stage managers. (1 credit per semester; may be repeated for credit; offered each semester.) Prerequisite: permission of the instructor.

title: Writing for Television
description: Combining workshop, lecture, class discussion, and in-class writing exercises, this course explores the fundamentals of the art and craft of writing for television. Over the length of the semester we will investigate the nature and meaning of "drama" and "visual narrative" as functioning on the small screen. We will do this in part through the examination of format, style, structure, and needs of the network/streaming sites for both a comedy (30 minute) and a drama (60 minute) series. We will also study the basics of scene building, conflict, character, and dialogue by writing a draft of both a “spec” script and an original pilot. Students will develop and complete an outline and first draft of a television pilot on their own and in collaborative groups. Same as ENG/FLM 387.

title: Gender, Sexuality, and Power
description: Using a gendered framework for analyzing diverse experiences, this broad core course in women’s, gender and sexuality studies explores basic concepts, methods of inquiry, and empirical studies from feminist perspectives, often in a global context. The course pays particular attention to how sexuality, race and ethnicity intersect with gender systems. WGS 210 is required for the WGSS major or minor and Joint Majors. Students who are considering a WGSS major or minor or Joint Major are urged to take WGS 210 early in their college career.

title: Hormones and Behavior
prereq: PSY 100 OR PERMISSION OR BIO 101 OR BIOP FOR MIN. SCORE OF Y
description: In this Biological Perspectives course, we’ll explore the role of hormones in three key areas of behavior: stress responses, sex, and relationships. How do hormones enable, regulate, or modify behavior in these contexts? How do behavior and the environment in turn affect hormone function? We’ll compare and contrast key theoretical models of hormones’ organization and activation effects based on human and animal studies to help us better understand our own behavior and give us insights into how culture and identity shape the kinds of research scientists pursue. Same as PSY237. Prerequisite: PSY100 or BIO101.

title: Nerd Problems: Race and Fandom
description: "Nerdy" interests such as anime, superhero franchises, video games, and computer savvy have not always been widely celebrated. Despite the mainstreaming of nerdy media products, toxic behaviors related to this arena of fandom persist. In studying films, tv shows, music, and memoirs, this class will explore how nerd culture provides a case study to explore gatekeeping and belonging based on racial categories, masculinity, femininity, and nationality. Same as AMS/AFS 274.

title: Romance & Politics of Pleasure
description: This course takes seriously the cultural work of romance novels, rom-coms, and other love stories. We consider how these texts and the scholarship about them address questions of gender, sexuality, and power. Same as AMS 277. Previously offered as AMS/WGS 377.

title: The Urban Citizen (CBL)
description: In this community-based learning course students will have the opportunity to engage in study and experiential activities around civic engagement and social issues. They will examine the lives of documented and undocumented citizens as well as “returning citizens” (who are formerly incarcerated) and newly arrived citizens. We will consider, among other things, gender and poverty, race relations, affordable housing, urban economies, crime and policing, schools, refugees, and environmentalism in an urban setting. Students will integrate their academic studies with direct community engagement work of their choice in Lancaster. Same as AMS/AFS/HIS 279.

title: Civil Rights & Civil Liberties
description: Explores civil rights and liberties in the American system, with emphasis on current problems and recent Court decisions. Prerequisite: GOV101 or GOV171 or GOV100. Same as GOV 315.

title: Civil Rights & Civil Liberties
description: Explores civil rights and liberties in the American system, with emphasis on current problems and recent Court decisions. Prerequisite: GOV101 or GOV171 or GOV100. Same as GOV 315.

title: Rights and Representations
description: This course explores controversies about the First Amendment (or freedom of expression), particularly in relation to race and gender, in the past and in the contemporary US. This class examines the categorical exceptions to the First Amendment and then focuses on the following case studies: hate speech in higher education, racial and sexual harassment in employment, and harassment in cyberspace. Same as AMS/GOV 358.

title: LGBT+ Human Rights in Chg Wrld
description: Are LGBT+ rights human Rights? Special rights? What protections do members of the LGBT+ community have? What protections should they have? How do countries vary in the protection or persecution of LGBT+ individuals? Utilizing data from the F&M Global Barometers (in addition to other sources), students will apply this knowledge to creating LGBT+ asylum profiles for various countries. Same as GOV370.

title: Fem Phil of Cognitive Science
prereq: WGS 210 AND (PHI 100 OR PHI 130 OR PHI 236 OR PHI 250 OR PSY 100 OR PERMISSION OR PSY 203 OR SPM 100 OR STS 136 )
description: This course considers feminist perspectives and projects within or in response to philosophy of mind, cognitive neuroscience, and cognitive science. What can we meaningfully say about “the mind,” “the brain,” “the body,” “gender,” “experience,” “perception,” or “identity” without considering insights from each? Or without interrogating who the “we” is that pronounces these ultimate truths of the human condition? In pursuing the potential relationship between these fields we develop interdisciplinary and critical thinking skills needed to improve our understanding of human cognition in the context of uneven and oppressive material, social, and political realities. One focus will be on the significance of intersectionality for newer movements both in feminist thinking and in cognitive science. Same as PHI/PSY372. Pre-reqs: WGS210 and (PHI100 or PHI130 or PHI236 or PHI250 or PSY100 or PSY203 or SPM100 or STS136) or permission of the instructor.

title: American Communities
description: This course focuses on the principal methods and paradigms used in conceptualizing, researching, and writing on “communities.” To do this we will focus on “community,” how communities vary in form and function, and what draws people into and away from various social groupings; we will study communities on their own terms, and within the wider context of American cultural and political life, with a special focus on F&M campus communities. Students will employ different methods in studying campus communities. Counts for the WGS major and minor. Not open to students who have taken AMS 350. Same as AMS/HIS 373.

title: Selling Sex
description: This seminar explores contemporary debates about law and policy surrounding commercial sex and also examines the history of commercial sex in the United States, including the local case study of "Lancaster Vice." We will study contemporary efforts to end human trafficking, particularly in relation to the criminalization of commercial sex. Same as AMS 474.

title: Global Reproductive Politics
description: This seminar introduces students to the history of sexuality and gender in Latin America as the study of identities and relationships of power that have changed over time. In addition to providing a foundation in current historical research and theoretical debates about sexuality as a category of analysis, the course will explore research methodologies using a wide range of sources, from censuses, oral accounts, diaries, letters, ecclesiastical accounts, judicial records, health reports, advertising, comic books, and other print media. It is useful to be able to read Spanish for this course, but not necessary. The seminar will emphasize the role of sexuality in the creation of diverse historical experiences of women and men, and its importance in the construction of varied masculinities and femininities within Latin America. The course will also explore how sexuality and gender have intersected with ethnicity, race, and social class in the creation of distinct Latin American societies and cultures. Same as HIS475. Prerequisite: HIS260 (recommended but not required).
